items.title: From assistants to companions: An exploratory mixed-methods study of AI chatbot adoption among Generation Z students in Thailand
items.abstract: This study explores how undergraduate Generation Z students at an international college in Thailand adopt and use AI chatbots. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a sensitizing framework, we conducted an exploratory convergent mixed-methods survey of 144 eligible students. Quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics and exploratory factor analysis of seven adoption items adapted from TAM and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), while qualitative analysis used LLM-assisted, researcher-verified coding of 127 and 117 substantive open-ended responses to examine motivations and desired features. The analysis suggested two provisional adoption-related dimensions, perceived relational value and social endorsement, and practical accessibility, although the factor-retention criteria were divided between one and two factors. Almost all students selected academic assistance as a reason for using AI chatbots (92.4%). Asked specifically about AI companions, students most often cited information seeking and convenience (27.6% of substantive responses), while personal and emotional support and reservations about companion use were raised in 20.5% and 19.7% of responses, respectively. Human-like interaction was the most frequently requested feature category (39.3%), followed by technical capabilities and academic tools such as citation support. The study contributes exploratory, cross-sectional evidence on AI chatbot adoption in a Thai higher-education context and highlights the importance of balancing practical utility, relational expectations, and clear human-AI boundaries.

items.title: From Exposure to Enactment: Distributed Accountability in AI Bias Analysis Tasks in English Writing for Academic Purposes
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into academic writing has raised ethical questions about intellectual property, authorship, and knowledge representation. Although existing research has examined academic integrity and AI literacy, how learners negotiate responsibility when responding to biased or culturally inappropriate AI‐generated outputs remains underexplored. Grounded in critical applied linguistics and informed by relational accountability and distributed agency, this study examines how students enacted accountability in an AI bias analysis task within an undergraduate English academic writing course at a Chinese university. Drawing on group reports, AI interaction records, reflective writing, field notes, and interviews, thematic analysis identified three interrelated orientations through which students enacted accountability: epistemic accountability (evaluating knowledge claims), relational accountability (negotiating responsibility across human‐AI relations), and ecological accountability (questioning the broader linguistic, cultural, and epistemic consequences of AI‐generated knowledge). These orientations reveal accountability as distributed across epistemic judgments, social and technological relations, and broader conditions of knowledge representation. We conceptualize this configuration as distributed accountability: a situated process through which learners negotiate and enact answerability for AI‐mediated knowledge and its consequences. By demonstrating this expansion of answerability, the study connects the micro‐ethics of classroom practice with the macro‐ethics of linguistic and epistemic diversity and equity in AI‐mediated knowledge production. It offers implications for future research on academic writing ethics, critical AI literacy, and educational AI governance in applied linguistics.

items.title: From Faculty Development to Health Professions Education: A 16-year Documentary Analysis in Myanmar Military Medical Education
items.abstract: Faculty development programmes must adapt to changing expectations in curriculum design, assessment, educational scholarship, technology, leadership and interprofessional practice. The Diploma in Medical Education (Dip. Med. Ed.) at the Defence Services Medical Academy (DSMA), Myanmar, provides a longitudinal example of such adaptation. In 2024, DSMA and the Military Institute of Nursing and Paramedical Sciences (MINP) combined their contributions to the programme, marking a new collaborative phase in its development. This study examined how the DSMA Dip. Med. Ed. programme changed between 2010 and 2026 and to identify the principal curricular and institutional transitions that moved it from foundational faculty development toward contemporary health professions education, including the development of DSMA-MINP collaboration from 2024. We conducted a retrospective documentary analysis using course handbooks from the first course in 2010-2011 through the 16th course handbook in 2026. A structured extraction framework examined programme aims, duration, curriculum architecture, teaching-learning strategies, educational technology, assessment, leadership, communication and professionalism, educational research, workshops and governance. The authors compared documents chronologically and synthesized recurring patterns and material changes into developmental phases. Five phases were identified: foundation and formalisation (2010-2013); consolidation of the modular faculty-development model (2014-2019); outcomes, constructive alignment and digitally supported delivery (2020-2023); DSMA-MINP collaboration and curricular expansion (2024-2025); and further curriculum modernisation (2026). The 2026 curriculum incorporated outcome-based and competency-based medical education, curriculum mapping, quality assurance and accreditation, interprofessional education, problem- and case-based learning, e-learning, simulation, artificial intelligence and AI ethics, educational governance, professionalism, research ethics and critical appraisal. The Dip. Med. Ed. retained a stable core mission while progressively broadening from teacher preparation to a more integrated health professions education programme. The combination of DSMA and MINP from 2024 and the subsequent curricular developments through 2026 represent important milestones in this transformation. Future evaluation should determine whether these intended curriculum changes translate into sustained changes in educational practice, scholarship and institutional outcomes.

items.title: From Global Landscapes to Local Contexts: A Bibliometric Analysis of Artificial Intelligence and Student Behavior
items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications has profound implications for higher education,including student behaviors, engagement, and productivity in learning. While academic literature addressing the implications of AI applications is on the rise, its relevance for fields of economics, business,and the social sciences remains disparate and localized. In this regard, this paper analyzes the bibliometric landscape of AI research using a set of indicators that include keyword co-occurrence, time and research density, and emerging research fronts using VOSviewer, and the search was limited to Scopus-indexed journal articles (2000-2025).A descriptive analysis was done based on three sets of documents, namely the global baseline, the discipline-specific body of work,and a local Malaysian dataset. The global dataset has produced a mature and integrated network with a primary emphasis on educational data mining and learning analytics.Nevertheless, temporal overlay visualization analysis reveals a sharp transition to the human and ethical factors surrounding generative artificial intelligence, including academic integrity and frameworks for evaluating teacher acceptance of disruptive technologies. In contrast, the Malaysian dataset was found to have a sparsely connected network, suggesting the growing nature of local research. Indeed, studies pertaining to Malaysia appear to focus on the interactions between students and ChatGPT and lack psychological theories in any of the included works.This study has identified the fundamental disconnect between regional and international research practices.As such, it can serve as the foundation for future studies that seek to understand the effects of artificial intelligence on the emotional,social, and academic development of students in developed digital economies.

items.title: From HPV Genetic Diversity to Precision Therapeutics: Viral-Host Interactions and Emerging Strategies for Cervical Cancer Prevention and Treatment
items.abstract: Cervical cancer is a major global health challenge, especially in low- and middle-income countries, despite the availability of effective prophylactic human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines, screening methods and established treatments. Cervical cancer is primarily caused by persistent infection with high-risk HPV, but persistent infection is necessary, but not sufficient, for the development of cancer. Advances in understanding HPV genetic diversity, viral persistence, and virus-host molecular interactions are creating new opportunities to improve precision in HPV prevention and treatment. HPV genotype distribution and differences in oncogenic potential inform vaccine development and screening strategies. The viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 disrupt host tumor-suppressor pathways, driving cellular immortalization and genomic instability. Molecular events such as viral insertion, epigenetic modifications, APOBEC-associated mutations, and immune escape contribute to disease progression. These discoveries have revealed molecular vulnerabilities that can be targeted therapeutically. Immune checkpoint inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates are used clinically in specific contexts of cervical cancer presentation and treatment. At the same time, therapeutic vaccines, adoptive cellular immunotherapies, RNA interference, and genome editing are being investigated as complementary strategies to target HPV-associated cervical cancer. With advances in next-generation sequencing, molecular biomarkers, and artificial intelligence, these tools could further refine risk stratification and therapy selection. This review explores the current understanding of HPV genetic variation and virus-host interactions driving a shift from traditional prevention and treatment strategies to precision prevention and targeted therapeutics, and critically assesses remaining challenges.

items.title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
items.abstract: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.

items.title: From Pilot to Production: A Seven-Check Readiness Framework for Deploying Generative and Agentic AI in the Enterprise
items.abstract: Many enterprise generative AI initiatives stall between a successful pilot and dependable production use. Industry forecasts suggest that at least 30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept, and that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. This paper argues that the gap is primarily a management and delivery problem rather than a model-capability problem, and proposes a practitioner framework for go-live decisions. The framework rests on a single organizing analogy, treating an AI system like a new hire, and translates it into seven readiness checks (value, ownership, data, evaluation, guardrails, operations and adoption), six hard stops that block launch regardless of overall score, an eight-part evidence pack, a 0–2 scoring rubric, and an additional control set for agentic systems that can take actions. The checks are mapped to established sources including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, and empirical work on machine learning engineering. Seven publicly documented cases are used to illustrate the failure modes each check is designed to catch. The paper closes with limitations and a proposed agenda for empirical validation. JEL classification: M15, O32, O33.

items.title: From Self-Confidence to Statistical Accuracy: Scaling Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation with Direct and LLM-Assisted Auditing
items.abstract: For large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), model-reported self-confidence is often miscalibrated, yet it may still be useful for efficient evaluation. At the same time, LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to direct human auditing, but its practical benefit depends on calibration quality and inference cost. This paper develops a unified statistical framework for both evaluation routes under alternative sampling strategies. For direct auditing, confidence-stratified sampling is used to recover population accuracy from partially verified outputs without requiring calibrated confidence. Finite-sample uncertainty is characterized, and the analysis shows how highly uneven confidence strata affect audit efficiency and label allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, the judge is modeled through sensitivity and false-positive rate, yielding an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty. The two routes are then compared through human-label and total-cost efficiency boundaries. Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro show that miscalibrated self-confidence can still support statistically valid stratified auditing. Under highly imbalanced confidence distributions, proportional allocation substantially reduces estimation error relative to equal-per-stratum allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, only a small subset of target--verifier pairs satisfies the idealized human-label efficiency condition, and automated inference costs can further limit potential savings. These findings clarify the statistical and economic conditions under which confidence-guided auditing and automated verification are useful.

items.title: From traditional employability skills to emerging AI competencies
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping graduate employability by changing how competencies are enacted, valued, and developed. While traditional employability frameworks identify competencies expected of graduates, limited research has examined how these competencies may be evolving within AI-enabled environments. This study examines established employability competency domains and explores faculty perceptions of emerging capability requirements in the age of generative AI. A sequential mixed-method design was adopted. Quantitative data from 177 graduating business students in Saudi Arabia were analysed using domain-level principal component analysis to assess the internal structure and reliability of seven established competency domains. Semi-structured interviews with twelve business faculty members were subsequently analysed thematically. The quantitative findings provide context-specific support for communication, leadership, critical thinking and problem-solving, teamwork, management capability, ICT capability, and professionalism. The qualitative findings identified three complementary patterns of perceived competency evolution: human-centric enduring competencies, AI-augmented competencies, and emerging AI-specific competencies. The findings suggest that AI-ready employability involves both the continuing relevance of established competencies and changes in how competencies are enacted alongside intelligent technologies. The study proposes an exploratory AI-ready employability framework integrating established competencies with perceived competency continuity, augmentation, and emergence, providing a foundation for further empirical investigation and curriculum development in AI-integrated higher education.

items.abstract: In light of Large Language Models (LLMs), which are drastically altering creative environments, this chapter addresses Hybrid Human-AI Collaboration Models. LLMs provide previously unheard-of skills in data analysis, content creation with sophisticated reasoning, their successful application requires a sophisticated awareness of their drawbacks, such as their vulnerability to bias, factual inaccuracies, and a lack of practical experience. In order to bridge this gap, hybrid models create organized frameworks that integrate the unique advantages of artificial and human intelligence in a complementary way. In this chapter different collaborative architectures, with an emphasis on models that range from AI-driven workflows with human oversight (where LLM directs the process and a human provides crucial validation and ethical correction) to AI augmentation (where the human is the primary decision-maker and LLM serves as an assistant). The ‘human-in-the-loop’ mechanism is essential to these models because it ensures accountability, quality control, and the application of ethical judgment and contextual knowledge—all of which are now outside the purview of even the most sophisticated LLMs. Through case studies that highlight best practices for task decomposition, interaction design, and performance measurements, the chapter explores the real-world applications of these concepts in domains such as technical writing, software development, and strategic decision-making. At last, hybrid models are needed to minimize LLM risks and for enabling new steps of creativity and productivity, deciding the movement of human-computer interaction in the generative AI.

items.title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
items.abstract: Many academic disciplines (in particular, mathematics and the theoretical sciences) face difficult questions about how to adapt their practices to the rise of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI). Before AI, a well-written research paper with a strong theoretical result acted as a reliable signal that its authors understood their field in depth. Now that AI is widely accessible, such signals have become cheaper to produce. As a result, they no longer reliably sort academics by their level of understanding. This has direct consequences for academic hiring. The age of AI raises a question for each side of the academic job market. Should an early-career researcher invest in a deep understanding of their field, or instead use AI to build a longer resume with many papers? Should a recruiter favor applicants with fewer papers who pass an interview aimed at probing understanding, or insist on both publication volume and a pass? In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model of this two-sided dilemma. We classify all pure-strategy equilibria that can arise in this game and use learning simulations to identify the behaviors that populations of applicants and recruiters may learn to adopt. Our analysis provides a framework for reasoning about how academic hiring can adapt to AI and for evaluating practices that preserve the value of deep understanding.

items.title: GenAI in Higher Education in the Context of East and South Asia: Current Trends and Stakeholders’ Perceptions
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education (HE) worldwide, yet evidence from Asia remains limited. This study examines how students, teachers, and other stakeholders in Asia perceive the role of GenAI in HE, identifying current usage trends and analysing how GenAI is incorporated into academic and pedagogical practices. Using a mixed methods design, the study gathered quantitative data through online surveys of undergraduate students and teachers. Qualitative insights were obtained through focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews with a sample of participants, including policymakers, educationists, I/NGO representatives, and IT sector professionals. Findings show that the research participants hold mixed views about the role of GenAI in HE, with some indications of integration into academic practices. The study provides insights into emerging GenAI practices in Asian HE and highlights implications for policy and pedagogical development.

items.title: Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
items.abstract: Research on coding agents mainly focuses on generation quality. Yet, safety-critical automotive software makes two additional demands. It prioritizes verification, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against industry standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR before it can be committed. It is also a narrow domain, written against layered architectures, embedded resource constraints, and organization-specific interface conventions that are scarce in the data general-purpose LLMs are trained on. We present a coding assistant for automotive C/C++ that addresses both demands. First, it exposes three tools to the user over the Model Context Protocol (generate, edit, and verify), allowing developers to run verify on any code on demand rather than relying on the agent to check its own output. Second, rather than using a general-purpose model, we customize the underlying LLM for the automotive domain through prompt engineering and fine-tuning. We construct a dataset from automotive production code of AUMOVIO, where each function is paired with the requirement texts and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior it must satisfy. In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers report verify as the most-used tool and confirm using it on their own code and not only on generated output. Comparing model customization strategies, 75% prefer the faster prompt-engineered configuration. MISRA- and AUTOSAR-inspired pattern checkers indicate that prompt engineering achieves a lower number of violations on C, while fine-tuning shows better conformance with architecture patterns for C++.

items.title: GENERATION GHOST: MODEL STRUKTURAL COGNITIVE OFFLOADING BERBASIS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TERHADAP ILLUSION OF COMPETENCE MELALUI CRITICAL THINKING PADA PELAJAR SMA DI MAKASSAR
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in learning enables students to delegate some cognitive processes to technology, a practice known as cognitive offloading. Although this practice may improve efficiency, using AI without critical evaluation may contribute to an illusion of competence, defined as a discrepancy between perceived understanding and actual performance. This study examined the relationship between AI-based cognitive offloading and the illusion of competence, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking among high school students in Makassar. A quantitative cross-sectional correlational design and purposive sampling were employed, involving 356 students aged 15–18 years. Cognitive offloading was measured using an adapted Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking using the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, and the illusion of competence through the discrepancy between Judgment of Learning and performance on an objective PISA-based test. Data were analyzed using Confirmatory Factor Analysis and path analysis in Mplus 8.4. The CFA results indicated acceptable measurement models for cognitive offloading and critical thinking. Path analysis showed that cognitive offloading was positively associated with the illusion of competence and negatively associated with critical thinking, while critical thinking was negatively associated with the illusion of competence. The significant indirect effect indicated complementary partial mediation. These findings highlight the importance of analyzing, evaluating, and verifying AI-generated output to support accurate judgments of understanding. ABSTRAK Penggunaan artificial intelligence (AI) generatif dalam pembelajaran memungkinkan pelajar menyerahkan sebagian proses kognitif kepada teknologi atau melakukan cognitive offloading. Meskipun meningkatkan efisiensi, penggunaan tanpa evaluasi kritis dapat menimbulkan illusion of competence, yaitu ketidaksesuaian antara keyakinan terhadap pemahaman dan performa aktual. Penelitian ini bertujuan menguji hubungan cognitive offloading berbasis AI dengan illusion of competence serta peran mediasi critical thinking pada pelajar SMA di Kota Makassar. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain cross-sectional correlational dan purposive sampling, melibatkan 356 pelajar berusia 15–18 tahun. Cognitive offloading diukur menggunakan adaptasi Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking menggunakan Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, sedangkan illusion of competence dioperasionalkan melalui ketidaksesuaian antara Judgment of Learning dan tes objektif berbasis PISA. Data dianalisis menggunakan Confirmatory Factor Analysis dan path analysis pada Mplus 8.4. Hasil CFA menunjukkan bahwa model pengukuran cognitive offloading dan critical thinking memiliki kesesuaian yang dapat diterima. Path analysis menunjukkan bahwa cognitive offloading berhubungan positif dengan illusion of competence dan negatif dengan critical thinking, sedangkan critical thinking berhubungan negatif dengan illusion of competence. Efek tidak langsung melalui critical thinking juga signifikan dan menunjukkan complementary partial mediation. Temuan ini menegaskan bahwa kemampuan menganalisis, mengevaluasi, dan memverifikasi keluaran AI merupakan bagian penting dalam menjaga ketepatan pelajar ketika menilai pemahamannya.

items.title: Generation Is Cheap, Selection Is Sovereign
items.abstract: Generative AI has made plausible output abundant and cheap, but plausibility is not evidence and evidence is not authority. Leading AI assistants already concede this in the notice beneath every prompt box, telling users the system can make mistakes and asking them to check — handing the work of verification to individuals without instruments, records or authority. This working paper proposes Computational Trust Engineering (CTE), an engineering discipline for the path from a language model’s completion to an organization’s consequence. It separates three selections that current practice collapses into one: a generative selection (which continuation is probable?), an evidentiary selection (which candidate is supportable?) and an authority selection (may the supported candidate produce consequence?). CTE grounds these in four realities (human, AI, actual and governance reality) and treats familiar failure modes as measurable gaps between them. It frames evidentiary selection as metrology, with the individual claim as the counted unit, “unknown” as a legitimate result, calibrated instruments and traceable provenance. It introduces attention as the allocation of scarce measurement effort, and states when a language model may serve as an instrument. The paper defends the three-layer separation through collapse analysis and precedent from internal control, functional safety and metrology. It also maps CTE to the NIST AI RMF, NIST AI 600-1, ISO/IEC 42001, assurance cases and the EU AI Act, and closes with deployment postures, five falsifiable hypotheses and a research agenda.

items.title: Generative AI and AI literacy in Elementary Education: A Systematic Review of Research published from 2021 to January 2026
items.abstract: This study explores how Generative AI has influenced research on AI literacy education at the elementary school level. A systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conducted to study implementations of Generative AI and methods of AI literacy education in elementary education. The review data includes 211 studies published from 2021 to January 2026 identified from SCOPUS, EBSCO, Web of Science, and Taylor & Francis. Thematic content analysis was used to identify and analyze themes in the review data to examine how the research field has developed after the release of Generative AI technology. The analysis identifies fundamental issues affecting the implementation of Generative AI in elementary education, including concerns about human interaction, varying approaches to ethical questions, and frequent concerns regarding the reliability of Generative AI outputs. The definition of the ethical dimensions of critical AI literacy is found to be inconclusive, calling for a broader adoption of critical AI literacy education at the elementary school level. Established use cases of Generative AI are identified, especially with self-regulated learning and foreign language studies. A holistic and integrated approach to AI literacy education for students and pre-service teachers is supported by the analysis. This study identifies research gaps for longitudinal research on Generative AI in elementary schools, parents’ role in students’ AI literacy, and a need to reach a scholarly consensus on the definition of AI ethics.

items.title: Generative AI and legal practice: a complicated relationship
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is widely expected to transform professional practices across multiple sectors, including the legal profession. This article critically examines the growing integration of GenAI tools into legal work and the implications this development carries for professional competence, ethical responsibility, and the broader institutional structure of legal practice. While AI promises substantial gains in efficiency by automating tasks such as legal research, document drafting, information retrieval, and data analysis, their adoption also raises significant concerns regarding reliability, transparency, confidentiality, and professional accountability. While prevailing narratives surrounding AI adoption in law often frame technological integration as both inevitable and normatively desirable, emphasising efficiency and competitive advantage while downplaying potential risks and value conflicts, the increasing delegation of professional tasks to algorithmic systems challenges traditional understandings of legal expertise, particularly in relation to judgement, reasoning, and professional autonomy. Moreover, unequal access to advanced AI tools and proprietary datasets may reinforce structural inequalities within the legal market, benefitting larger firms while disadvantaging smaller practices. This article argues for a balanced approach that combines technological literacy with strong ethical frameworks and institutional safeguards. Ultimately, responsible integration of GenAI requires sustained human oversight and collective professional engagement to ensure that technological innovation supports, rather than undermines, the core values of legal practice.

items.title: Generative AI as an external knowledge source: digital literacy, individual absorptive capacity and sports communication knowledge creation intention
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how knowledge-oriented generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tool use (GAIU) is associated with sports communication knowledge creation intention (SCKCI), with digital literacy (DL) and individual absorptive capacity (IAC) as sequential capability pathways. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 616 university students in Yunnan Province, China, with sport-related academic backgrounds or sports communication experience was analysed using confirmatory factor analysis, latent-variable structural equation modelling and 5,000 resample bootstrap mediation. Composite-score mediation served as a robustness check. Findings Both specific indirect paths and the sequential GAIU–DL–IAC–SCKCI path were significant, while the direct association remained significant, yielding a pattern consistent with partial sequential mediation. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, self-reported and region-specific design does not establish causal or temporal ordering and limits generalisability. items.title: Generative AI Powered by Large Language Models for Leadership Development: Between Epistemic Responsibility and the Future of Innovation
items.abstract: This chapter examines language-based generative AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), as active epistemic agents in leadership development. Moving beyond their perceived neutrality, the authors argue that LLMs serve as mirrors of dominant assumptions, co-constructors of leadership meaning, and framing devices of legitimate knowledge. The sources highlight how these systems reinforce prevailing Euro-American managerial ideals, often marginalizing diverse leadership paradigms such as Indigenous, collectivist, or spiritual frameworks, thereby amplifying structural and cultural biases. Through epistemic feedback loops and personalization, LLMs can subtly shape leadership identity and constrain developmental horizons, leading to adaptive standardization or performative conformity. The chapter emphasizes the critical need for epistemic responsibility in innovation leadership, advocating for leaders to interrogate system framings, reflect on their influence, and cultivate design awareness. This involves fostering inclusive data practices, participatory design methodologies, and culturally responsive AI governance to ensure AI-mediated innovation ecosystems are just, inclusive, and reflect pluralistic worldviews. Ultimately, the chapter calls for leaders to reclaim framing power and engage AI dialogically to foster an innovation leadership that is reflexive, ethically grounded, and attuned to human complexities.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Generative AI-Driven Marketing Content Generation and User Response Prediction
items.abstract: This paper presents a generative AI-driven framework designed for e-commerce brand marketing, which integrates marketing content generation with user response prediction. By combining product information, brand characteristics, user behavior data, and contextual information, the framework generates semantically aligned marketing content and predicts user responses, such as click-through rates and purchase intentions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several baseline models in content generation and user response prediction tasks. The framework provides practical support for personalized marketing, content delivery, and decision-making. Moreover, it exhibits strong robustness under challenging scenarios, such as missing user data and content perturbation. This study highlights the potential of generative AI for optimizing both content creation and marketing performance in digital commerce environments.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence reshapes university students' sustainable use of academic information resources: mixed evidence from behavioral logs and perceptual survey data
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how students retrieve and consume academic information, yet whether it substitutes for or complements library resources remains contested, and prior surveys rarely separate auxiliary from substitutive use. Methods This study uses a convergent triangulation design that combines multiple quantitative methods. It addresses the same set of research propositions by collecting perceptual-level questionnaire data and behavioral-level logs and platform usage statistics, analyzing them independently, and comparing the findings at the interpretation stage. Using 368 student questionnaires, we test an auxiliary-substitutive dual-path structural equation model and compare the results with an interrupted time-series analysis of 3.2 million print-loan logs (2017-2025) and digital-platform statistics from 2021 to the first half of 2026. Results Print-resource continuance intention is positively associated with deep-reading demand, but not significantly associated with auxiliary GenAI use. Survey results showed auxiliary GenAI use positively associated with digital-resource continuance intention, yet insufficiently distinct from perceived digital-resource convenience; platform data showed nascent use of embedded AI features. Substitutive GenAI use shows only a weak negative association with print-resource continuance intention, while the nine-year loan record reveals no significant level or trend change at the January 2023 breakpoint; task-channel fit shows no significant moderating effect. Discussion In this institution, findings align more with dual-channel coexistence than with the “AI-replaces-libraries” narrative; the survey-level substitution association has not yet appeared in aggregate borrowing behavior, informing collection development, service redesign, and AI-literacy education.

items.title: Global Trends of Artificial Intelligence Applications in Family Medicine: A Comprehensive Scopus-Based Bibliometric Analysis (2016–2026)
items.abstract: Aim: To map recent artificial intelligence research in family medicine and primary care against an earlier 2015–2024 bibliometric baseline. Methods: Scopus was searched on 9 July 2026 for 2016–2026 publications. One researcher screened 3452 articles and reviews; 132 topical and 13 language exclusions left 3307 records. Manual title, DOI, and Scopus-identifier checks identified no duplicates. VOSviewer 1.6.21 and Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix 5.4.1; R 4.6.1) supported descriptive analysis and mapping. Results: Output increased from 531 in 2024 to 792 in 2025 (49.2%). The 2025 and partial 2026 component contained 1407 records (42.5%); 615 were dated 2026. The USA led publication and raw citation rankings (711 publications; 18,671 citations), while China preceded the United Kingdom in publication count. The Journal of Medical Internet Research (78 publications) and Scientific Reports (69) led the venues; seven top ten venues were shared with the earlier study. Language model terminology coexisted with later-positioned explainability, risk stratification, and diagnostic accuracy terms. Conclusions: This updated map quantifies post-2024 activity and identifies continuity and corpus-dependent differences in geography, dissemination, and evaluation-related vocabulary. Single-database and English language coverage, single-researcher screening, unadjusted citations, and incomplete 2026 coverage limit inference. The findings describe research activity, not clinical adoption, safety, effectiveness, or causality.

items.title: Governance as the Key Question of the Coming Years: A Scholarly Dialogue With Guilherme Canela on Freedom of Expression, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of Information Governance
items.abstract: In this scholarly dialogue for Media, Technology, and Governance , Guilherme Canela reflects on the centrality of governance in contemporary debates over media, technology, and the global information ecosystem. Drawing on his long-standing work with journalists, governments, civil society, regulators, judges, researchers, and international organizations, Canela situates freedom of expression, access to information, and digital transformation within a broader human rights framework. The conversation begins with Canela's professional trajectory from Latin America to UNESCO headquarters in Paris, then turns to the challenges posed by generative artificial intelligence, platform power, journalism's economic viability, and the need for multistakeholder governance. Canela argues that although technologies change, the principles of journalism, human rights, transparency, accountability, and meaningful participation remain essential. He also calls for scholars to study information and journalism as public goods, the growing attacks on accountability systems, and the ways academic evidence can inform policymaking without sacrificing independence. The dialogue concludes with a message to researchers: governance is the key topic of the coming years, and the academic community is needed to provide the evidence, concepts, and critical debate required to meet that challenge.

items.title: GPDPO: Learning from Reward Conflicts via Group Pareto-Dominance Policy Optimization
items.abstract: Multi-reward reinforcement learning offers a promising framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with diverse objectives, but conflicting reward signals can induce ambiguous update directions and hinder stable optimization. Existing approaches address such conflicts through reward reweighting, gradient coordination, or rollout filtering, yet they primarily operate on per-response or group-level optimization signals and underexploit relational information among sampled responses. As a result, conflict-filtered rollouts may still contain useful supervision that is discarded during training. We propose Group Pareto-Dominance Policy Optimization (GPDPO), a multi-reward policy optimization method that recovers pairwise supervision from conflict-filtered rollouts. GPDPO identifies Pareto-dominance relations among sampled responses and converts them into auxiliary preference signals, which are jointly optimized with the original policy objective. This enables more effective reuse of existing rollouts without additional sampling or reward evaluation. Experiments on API-Bank across multiple model scales and reward configurations show that GPDPO consistently outperforms competitive multi-reward optimization baselines. Further analysis demonstrates that GPDPO reduces both group-relative and pairwise reward conflicts, supporting the effectiveness of exploiting relational supervision for multi-reward alignment. Code will be released.

items.title: Greater adoption of artificial intelligent tools requires resolution of the liability conundrum
items.abstract: Clinician-facing artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tools can benefit patient care, but also have potential to cause physical or psychological patient harm. Opinions differ among stakeholders on who should be held responsible when such events occur – the clinician, the developer or vendor, the deploying institution, or some combination. Under current Australian tort law, clinicians remain primarily responsible for patient harm, even if software is shown to be flawed. As a result, clinicians may avoid or delay using AI tools despite demonstrated benefits to patient care. We briefly describe unique legal challenges posed by the use of AI tools, propose a framework for sharing liability among all parties according to their contribution to AI-related harm, and, failing this, offer nine strategies that clinicians and health services can adopt now to lower their liability risk.

items.title: Green and Sustainable Computing: Efficient Strategies, Best Practices, and Emerging Research Trends
items.abstract: Green and sustainable computing has evolved from a narrow focus on reducing the energy consumed by computer hardware into a broader discipline concerned with energy efficiency, distributed architectures, artificial intelligence, environmental impact, and lifecycle sustainability. This paper presents a structured review and trend analysis based on the findings reported in a recent large-scale study of 11,119 Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 1960 and 2025. The reviewed study used BERTopic with transformer-based embeddings, UMAP dimensionality reduction, HDBSCAN clustering, and temporal analysis to identify 36 research topics. This paper reorganizes those findings into an IJARSCT-style review format and synthesizes the major research directions, thematic groups, developmental stages, challenges, and future opportunities. The evidence shows that virtualization and hardware-efficiency themes have historically been important, while edge computing, AI-supported systems, neuromorphic architectures, UAV computing, and environmentally aware computation have gained research attention. The review also highlights limitations associated with database coverage, metadata quality, topic interpretation, and the use of relative topic prevalence. The resulting framework can help students and researchers understand the changing landscape of green computing and identify areas for further investigation.

items.title: Health policy at your fingertips? Mapping and evaluation of existing digital health policy repositories.
items.abstract: Background Digital repositories and databases facilitate faster dissemination, transparency, and stakeholder collaboration. This review aimed to map and evaluate such digital infrastructures, focusing on their scope, content, functionality, adherence to FAIR (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability and Reuse) principles, and user interface and experiences (UI/UX). Methods A review of global digital health policy repositories was conducted across multiple search engines and databases. The review targeted digital repositories that systematically collate health policy documents at a global level. Two country-specific repositories with a bearing on global health policies were also included. Results The study identified 59 global health policy repositories, with 15 matching our inclusion criteria evaluated in detail. These repositories contain vast amounts of data and are generally freely accessible, rendering them immensely rich sources for health policy documents, though with significant variability in content and coverage. The majority have a health focus, including HIV/AIDS, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH); about a third are broader and more emerging health threats are often neglected. Accessibility and usability are limited, with basic UI features such as search and filtering tools are present for almost all repositories and a notable lack of advanced analytics or artificial intelligence capabilities. Furthermore, many repositories struggle to adhere to FAIR principles, reducing their utility and potential for integration. Sustainability is also a concern, as funding often relies on short-term projects or philanthropic support, undermining long-term viability. Conclusion These issues collectively hinder the ability of digital health policy repositories to support comprehensive and timely global health policy development. To unlock the full potential of existing or new repositories for health policy, identified challenges should be tackled systematically. We provide specific recommendations aimed at driving the development of equitable, inclusive, high-functioning repositories and strengthening evidence-driven global health policy systems.

items.title: Heterogeneity and Subgrouping in Modern Statistics and AI
items.abstract: Heterogeneity is a defining feature of modern data: individuals, subpopulations, sites, modalities, tasks, and time points may differ in distributions, associations, treatment effects, or decision objectives. This review develops a unified perspective in which heterogeneous analysis is a problem of structured information borrowing: deciding what should be shared, what should remain distinct, and how uncertainty about that structure should enter inference and decisions. We connect classical stratification, interaction models, finite mixtures, mixed-effects models, and empirical Bayes with subgroup discovery, individualized learning, synthetic data generation, large language models, federated learning, privacy, security, and mobile health. Precision medicine provides a central example: subgroup rules offer interpretable approximations to individualized response surfaces, whereas partially pooled models stabilize patient-specific estimation. Across applications, the same tensions recur: population averages can conceal consequential variation, unrestricted personalization is unstable, adaptive subgroup discovery creates selection bias, and borrowing across incompatible sources causes negative transfer. These difficulties are amplified in contemporary AI, where sparse user histories, entangled representations, heterogeneous preferences, feedback loops, distribution shift, and privacy constraints make reliable personalization and evaluation especially challenging. We conclude with an agenda for calibrated personalization that integrates multilevel representations, selective borrowing, subgroup-aware evaluation, and valid uncertainty quantification.

items.title: Higher Education's Fourth Disruption and the Need for Resilient, Continual Crisis Leadership
items.abstract: Higher education is confronting its fourth major disruption within a single career arc, one defined not by a single policy shift or budget crisis but by a deep cultural reckoning. Over the past 30 years, 3 technological revolutions, the Internet, the smartphone, and generative artificial intelligence (AI), have systematically collapsed distance, time, and trust. Rather than transform in response, higher education layered new technologies atop legacy structures, raising costs and eroding public credibility. Today, the sector faces a collapse of legitimacy, fueling political interventions and public skepticism. This chapter argues that surviving and leading through this era requires more than strategic planning or operational efficiency. It demands a posture of resilient, continual crisis leadership grounded in human connection. Drawing from decades of leadership experience across multiple institutions and crises, Timothy Chester offers six practical strategies designed to rebuild trust and guide institutions through ongoing volatility. In an age where disruption is a permanent condition, this chapter serves as both a warning and a field guide, calling leaders to embrace clarity, compassion, and steady presence as higher education navigates its most profound test yet.

items.title: HiLO: Towards Product-Level Graceful Degradation with a Quality-Aware, Load-Aware Control Framework
items.abstract: Graceful degradation is a key mechanism employed by large-scale systems to handle overload conditions. Its importance has grown further as GPU-intensive LLM inference introduces persistent capacity constraints that cannot be addressed through provisioning alone. Common degradation approaches rely on service-level mechanisms such as load shedding and circuit breakers, or on feature-level switches (some manually controlled) to preserve availability and quality. While effective at protecting services, such approaches lead to untestable product states and thereby unpredictable product quality. We present HiLO (High Load Optimizer), an automated product-level degradation system designed to handle graceful degradation at scale. HiLO maps observed load to a product state lattice: a small set of pre-validated product states, partially ordered by degradation severity. Dependencies are resolved at design time enabling deterministic and continuous control without requiring runtime dependency discovery. The same abstraction applies unchanged across heterogeneous services, including GPU-intensive deep models, LLMs and their serving layers. At Microsoft, HiLO is deployed in Bing (serving over a billion monthly active users), where it manages on average two traffic surges per week across all datacenters, bounding OneDCG (relevance) drop to under 0.5 points (the operational target) even under sustained load exceeding 2$\times$ baseline peak. HiLO complements existing service-level protections with product-level coordination and makes product quality measurable, testable and predictable.

items.title: How do learning facilitation competency and self-leadership relate to learning outcomes?
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to empirically examine how instructors’ learning facilitation competency and learners’ self-leadership are associated with engagement, satisfaction and transfer in corporate training contexts. It further investigates whether learning engagement mediates the relationships among these key variables. Design/methodology/approach The research was conducted with a sample of 537 adult learners who had prior experience in corporate training programs and was grounded in facilitation learning theory and self-directed learning theory. Findings The findings show that instructors’ facilitation competency is significantly associated with learning engagement and satisfaction but does not show a significant direct relationship with learning transfer. Learners’ self-leadership is positively associated with all three outcomes: engagement, satisfaction and transfer. Learning engagement functions as a key mediator, especially between facilitation competency and transfer. Overall, facilitation competency shows stronger associations with engagement and satisfaction than self-leadership. Research limitations/implications This study has several limitations. First, cross-sectional self-report data limits causal inference and common method bias may inflate associations, particularly for learning transfer. Second, the sample is limited to Korean adult learners, which may affect generalizability across cultural contexts. Third, organizational variables – such as supervisor support, learning climate and transfer opportunities – were not included, though these are known predictors of transfer. Future research should adopt longitudinal or experimental designs, incorporate organizational-level variables, replicate findings across diverse cultural contexts and reexamine discriminant validity between self-leadership and learning engagement. Practical implications Findings suggest that both instructor facilitation and learner self-leadership matter for training effectiveness. Organizations should invest in developing instructors’ facilitation competencies – not just content expertise – to foster engagement and satisfaction. Equally, training programs should be designed to strengthen learners’ self-leadership skills, as these are associated with engagement, satisfaction and transfer. Since learning engagement emerged as a key mediator, instructional strategies that deepen active participation are likely to improve training outcomes. Psychologically safe learning climates and structured instructor development are essential for transfer-oriented instruction. Social implications When instructors move beyond simply delivering content and truly function as learning facilitators, learners develop the capacity to think for themselves, adapt to new challenges and apply what they have learned in meaningful ways. Corporate training must not stop at learning – what matters is whether that learning carries over into practice and shows up in organizational outcomes. By investing in facilitation competency and learner self-leadership, organizations can cultivate workforces capable of continuous adaptation. In an AI-driven era, human facilitation remains irreplaceable for fostering autonomous, transfer-ready learners. Originality/value These results provide empirical support for Rogers’ (1969) assertion that instructors, when functioning as facilitators rather than one-way deliverers of knowledge, foster meaningful learning experiences. Ultimately, this study offers both theoretical and practical implications for improving learner satisfaction and instructional effectiveness in workplace learning contexts.

items.title: Human Skin Disease Detection
items.abstract: Skin diseases are common health conditions that affect people worldwide. Early detection and accurate classification of skin diseases are important for supporting timely medical treatment. However, identifying skin diseases through visual examination can be challenging because different skin conditions may have similar visual characteristics. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence and deep learning have created opportunities to develop computer-aided systems for medical image analysis. This research focuses on human skin disease detection using deep learning techniques. The proposed approach uses skin images as input and applies image preprocessing techniques to prepare the images for classification. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can automatically extract important features such as colour, texture, and lesion patterns. Residual Networks (ResNet) can also be used to learn complex image features through their residual connections, supporting the classification of different skin conditions. The system aims to identify patterns in skin images and classify them into predefined disease categories based on the training data. The performance of the proposed approach can be assessed using evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. This research explores the potential of deep learning to support preliminary skin disease screening and improve the efficiency of image-based analysis. items.title: Human Tolerance to Injury
items.abstract: Biomechanics is an interdisciplinary field which combines physics, mechanical engineering, and life sciences to understand the relationship of physical forces to the functioning of the human body. A very important concept of biomechanics is that of human tolerance: there are quantifiable limits to the human's ability to withstand physical forces without harm. If these limits are exceeded, reversible or irreversible injury will occur. Vehicles and equipment can be designed such that even if a vehicle is involved in a crash the, resulting injuries are minimized or eliminated. Principles of ergonomics can be used to make equipment easier to use, more efficient, less tiring, and therefore safer.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration and Innovation in Corporate Communication Models: A Study of Intelligent Transformation Based on University-Industry-Research Collaboration
items.abstract: This study investigates how human-AI collaboration reshapes corporate communication models within intelligent transformation, focusing on university–industry–research collaboration as an enabling mechanism. Drawing on qualitative case evidence and framework development, the paper identifies three collaborative modes-co-design, adaptive integration, and evaluative feedback-that mediate between AI capabilities and organizational communication innovation. The findings suggest that successful intelligent transformation depends less on technology adoption than on the institutional alignment of academic knowledge, industrial practice, and research-driven experimentation. Corporate communication evolves from linear information dissemination to dynamic stakeholder engagement, with human oversight and ethical judgment embedded in AI-supported workflows. The paper contributes a framework linking university–industry–research inputs, human-AI collaboration modes, and communication performance, and concludes with implications for policy and managerial practice.

items.title: Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Nursing: Clinical Augmentation, Therapeutic Relationships, and Responsible Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering mental health nursing through prediction, natural language processing, digital phenotyping, conversational agents, and generative documentation. This integrative narrative review examines how these functions can support care while preserving therapeutic relationships, recovery, professional accountability, and patient rights. A targeted literature and regulatory update was completed on October 26, 2026; the revised bibliography comprises 35 sources, including six contemporary nursing or nursing-education reviews. Sources were synthesized thematically, without pooled effects or a claim of exhaustive systematic retrieval. Recent reviews establish substantial conceptual overlap and identify persistent limitations in external validity, person-centred outcomes, sustained engagement, and implementation evidence. Accordingly, this article contributes an author-developed nurse-led implementation and assurance framework that connects relational nursing theory, sociotechnical safety, evidence maturity, intended-use risk, and Brazilian governance. Operational requirements include calibration, prevalence-sensitive predictive values, prospective silent validation, measurable escalation, competent human review, abstention, version control, incident grading, and controlled revalidation. Documentation benefits must be assessed through total verification workload and protected therapeutic time. The risk matrix is a conceptual proposal, not a validated clinical instrument or binding legal classification. The framework has not been prospectively evaluated. AI adoption is defensible only when local evidence, service capacity, equity, privacy, and patient choice support the intended use; technical performance alone cannot establish clinical benefit.

items.title: Hybrid retrieval–verification framework for hallucination reduction in medical LLMs
items.abstract: Clinicians use Large Language Models (LLMs) for clinical decision support, medical question answering, and automated document writing. However, these models can hallucinate and pose safety risks. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factuality, it does not always produce outputs consistent with supporting evidence. To address these issues, this study reframes NLI-based unsupported-response rate mitigation for generative models as a confidence-aware inference problem and proposes a unified CARE-Med framework for retrieval, generation, and verification. The framework ensures the reliability of its outputs by leveraging dense retrieval, natural language inference verifiers, and a confidence scoring mechanism. The authors validated the anti-NLI-based unsupported-response optimisation method for biomedical large models proposed in this paper against the MIMIC-III, PubMedQA, and BioASQ benchmarks. The method reduces NLI-based unsupported-response rate decreases from 32% for the Baseline LLM to 10% for CARE-Med, corresponding to a 22-percentage-point or 68.8% relative reduction. Compared with conventional RAG, NLI-based unsupported-response rate decreases from 21% to 10%, corresponding to an 11-percentage-point or 52.4% relative reduction. The authors leverage explicit verification and uncertainty reasoning to meet requirements for safe clinical deployment.

items.title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
items.abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

items.title: Identifying the Opportunities and Challenges of Using Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnosis, Initial Management, and Triage of Trauma Patients in Pre-Hospital Emergency Care: A Qualitative Meta-Synthesis Study
items.abstract: Background: This research aimed to analyze and identify the opportunities and challenges of applying artificial intelligence (AI) in the pre-hospital emergency setting for the diagnosis, initial management, and triage of trauma patients.The objective is to provide a practical roadmap for the policymaking and safe implementation of this technology.Methods: This qualitative study was conducted using a meta-synthesis (research synthesis) approach.A systematic search was performed in major scientific databases to identify original articles published between 2015 and 2026 (1394-1404 in the Iranian calendar).After screening the studies based on the PRISMA guidelines, data from the eligible articles were extracted using a structured checklist and analyzed through thematic content analysis (TCA).The trustworthiness of the findings was assessed and confirmed according to Lincoln and Guba's criteria.Results: Out of a total of 221 retrieved articles, 24 eligible studies were included in the analysis.The findings indicated that AI application, on one hand, possesses significant potential to transform clinical and operational processes.These potentials include enhancing triage accuracy, intelligent patient monitoring, decision support, logistics optimization, and efficient documentation.On the other hand, realizing these opportunities is contingent upon overcoming a wide range of obstacles, including data and information issues, infrastructural and technical limitations, algorithmic constraints, human and organizational barriers, and ethical and legal considerations.Conclusion: Although AI, by enabling intelligent monitoring and improving triage accuracy, has the potential to revolutionize the management of the "golden hour" in trauma care, its implementation is confronted with five multifaceted categories of challenges.The results indicate that the successful translation of these opportunities into sustainable clinical practice cannot be achieved solely through technological advancement; rather, it requires systemic transformation, an integrated approach, and the adoption of evidence-based policies to simultaneously address infrastructural, human, and legal barriers.

items.title: IDIOMATICITY AND AI – WORK-RELATED PHRASEOLOGICAL UNITS IN BULGARIAN AND THEIR TRANSLATION EQUIVALENTS IN ENGLISH
items.abstract: In a world where technology is rapidly gaining popularity and is increasingly fulfilling various functions, the issue of machine translation is also becoming a matter of importance. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is quickly turning into a necessity as far as speed and accuracy are concerned. And if AI translation tools come in handy in almost all spheres of rendition from a source (SL) to a target language (TL), there are some challenges when transferring certain types of phrases, sentences and texts. With the assistance of AI tools, translation is becoming a quicker way to handle general phrases, language chunks and texts, yet a personal knowledge of culture and culture-specific competence is needed when phraseological units are concerned. They are culturally-bound units, whereby linguistic knowledge, lexical fluency and ready-made grammatical constructions are not enough to accurately convey the message of the unit. A knowledge of the culture, background and ideology of a social group or people is necessary so as to achieve adequate rendition of ideas and thoughts. Researchers (Mercan, 2024; Shalevska, 2025) have placed the importance of MT, yet they have focused on the significance of the human factor as well. The current study is thus an attempt to delve into the matter of translating phraseological units from Bulgarian into English with the assistance of AI translation tools, thus unveiling the degree to which they can be serviceably and relevantly transferred from one language into another and seeing as to what extent the meaning behind the units has been preserved.

items.title: IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE APPLICATIONS ON PERSONALIZED COSMETIC SHOPPING EXPERIENCE ON SHOPEE E-COMMERCE PLATFORM IN VIETNAM
items.abstract: The authors investigated the impact of Artificial Intelligence on the personalized cosmetic shopping experience on the Shopee e-commerce platform in Viet Nam. The team proposed seven hypotheses examining how AI-related factors influence user satisfaction. A quantitative approach was used, with survey data collected from 229 respondents and analyzed via SPSS 22. Results indicate that five factors - Personalization Risk Management, Perceived Usefulness, Trust Level, Customer Behavior Recognition, and User Data Quality- have significant positive effects on user satisfaction. At the same time, the quality of Machine Learning Algorithms, when applied mechanically without domain-specific calibration, has a statistically significant negative effect. These findings contribute a novel empirical perspective on AI adoption in a high-involvement product category to offer practical recommendations for platform developers, cosmetic sellers, and regulatory authorities.

items.title: Impact of artificial intelligence on medical education: applications, benefits and challenges
items.abstract: This research explores the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on medical education, highlighting its applications, benefits, and challenges.AI has revolutionized medical teaching through tools such as advanced clinical simulations, intelligent tutoring systems, AI-assisted diagnostics, and automated assessments.These technologies enable personalized, safe, and efficient learning, enhancing the acquisition of clinical and diagnostic skills.Additionally, immediate feedback and the ability to practice in virtual environments without risking patient safety are significant benefits.However, the implementation of AI faces challenges such as data privacy, high costs, unequal accessibility, and the need for faculty training.The risk of technological dependency and the potential loss of essential soft skills in medical practice are also discussed.The essay concludes that while AI offers transformative opportunities, its integration must be carefully managed to ensure it complements, rather than replaces, human clinical judgment.The importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and ongoing research is emphasized to maximize the benefits of AI in medical education.

items.title: Impact of confidentiality assurances and self-disclosure on user satisfaction with AI-assisted emotional support
items.abstract: Purpose While AI conversational agents such as Woebot offer a promising avenue for improving psychological well-being through empathetic conversations with nonclinical populations, growing privacy breach risks of AI are a significant threat to their use for emotional support. Therefore, this study aims to examine how confidentiality assurances from AI agents affect user satisfaction with AI-assisted emotional support, exploring the serial-mediation effects of perceived confidentiality and self-disclosure and the moderation effect of privacy concerns. Design/methodology/approach In a controlled experiment, 350 US adults interacted with a standardized AI emotional support agent in a three-dimensional metaverse and were randomly assigned to either the confidentiality-assurance condition or the control condition. Findings Results showed that confidentiality assurances significantly increased user satisfaction with AI-assisted emotional support. Moreover, we observed the mediation effects of perceived confidentiality and the serial-mediation effects of both perceived confidentiality and willingness to self-disclose. Originality/value This study contributes to the privacy literature by exploring how brief, standardized confidentiality assurances function in an AI-driven emotional support context. Instead of focusing on complex, personalized privacy designs, these findings offer a nuanced perspective on human-AI interactions that a simple structural cue can serve as a sufficient heuristic anchor to strengthen users' willingness to self-disclose across varying user traits.

items.title: Impact of Mindfulness Training on PTSD Symptoms and Sleep Quality in a Cohort of Firefighters
items.abstract: Introduction: Firefighters are frequently exposed to traumatic occupational experiences, which may adversely affect their mental health and sleep quality. This study aimed to investigate the effect of a mindfulness-based intervention on post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and sleep quality among firefighters in Shiraz, Iran. Methods: This quasi-experimental study employed a pre-test, post-test, and two-month follow-up design. A convenience sample of 70 male trauma-exposed firefighters was recruited (2023–2024). Participants were assigned to either a mindfulness intervention group (n=31; M_age=32.00±4.10) or a control group (n=34; M_age=30.65±3.59). The intervention group received an eight-session (90 minutes/week) mindfulness program, while the control group received no intervention. Assessments utilized the Mississippi Scale for Combat-Related PTSD (M-PTSD) and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Data were analyzed using MANCOVA and ANCOVA (SPSS v.28). Results: The mindfulness group demonstrated significant improvements in sleep quality (pre- test: 9.61, post-test: 5.10, follow-up: 5.74) and PTSD symptoms (pre-test: 100.29, post-test: 92.97, follow-up: 94.29) compared to the control group (p<0.001). Multivariate and univariate analyses of covariance confirmed that the intervention group exhibited significantly lower adjusted mean scores for both variables at post-test and follow-up. Conclusion: Mindfulness intervention significantly reduced PTSD symptoms and improved sleep quality among firefighters. These findings suggest that mindfulness training is a viable strategy for stress management and mental well-being in this population. Policymakers are encouraged to integrate mindfulness-based programs into occupational health services for firefighters

items.title: Improved ultrasound diagnosis of lateral lymph node metastasis in papillary thyroid carcinoma through integrated artificial intelligence (AI)-driven multimodal analysis
items.abstract: Lateral lymph node metastasis (LLNM) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) significantly impacts PTC prognosis and treatment strategies. This study aimed to develop and validate a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI)-driven integrated model to predict LLNM by combining clinical data, radiomics features, and deep learning-based imaging features. A cohort of 1566 patients was divided into training, validation, and test sets. To indirectly assess LLNM risk based on tumor aggressiveness characteristics, radiomics features were extracted from ultrasound images of the primary thyroid tumor and selected using Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression to construct a support vector machine (SVM) model. Clinical variables were used for logistic regression. Deep learning features characterizing the primary thyroid nodule were derived from the TResNet model, and these predictions were integrated into a multimodal model and evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. The integrated model outperformed individual models, achieving the highest area under the curve in the training (0.984), validation (0.943), and test (0.951) datasets. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified key predictive factors such as TResNet scores, SVM-based radiomics features, tumor size, location, sex, and thyroglobulin antibody levels. After incorporating the model, the diagnostic accuracy was enhanced for ultrasound physicians at all levels (junior, medium, and senior), with significant improvements in sensitivity, specificity, and confidence. The proposed AI-driven integrated model, which predicts LLNM risk by analyzing primary thyroid tumor characteristics, demonstrated robust predictive performance and clinical utility in LLNM risk stratification for PTC patients. It significantly improves diagnostic accuracy compared to individual models, providing a non-invasive, personalized tool to support clinical decision-making.

items.title: Improving Instruction Hierarchy by Learning from Goal-Goal Conflicts
items.abstract: The recent incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure illustrates the importance of instruction hierarchy (IH): an LLM should follow lower-priority instructions, such as user requests, only when they do not conflict with higher-priority instructions, such as system policies. IH can be effectively improved by fine-tuning LLMs on simulated examples of instruction conflicts, whose diversity is key to teaching LLMs to properly handle conflicts at test time. However, our decomposition of a task into goals and constraints reveals a conflict type -- goal-goal conflicts -- that is absent from existing IH training sets from OpenAI and NVIDIA. We show the importance of this conflict type: fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B-it on examples of this conflict type significantly improves IH on a wide range of real-world tasks unseen in training; adding these examples to existing IH training sets for fine-tuning also gives better IH adherence. The IH gains come with trivial mean utility changes on no-conflict tasks across eight benchmarks. Our work advocates including this new conflict type in IH training, even if these examples do not reflect typical LLM use.
