items.title: Improving VLMs on Scientific Chart Analysis via Autonomous Evolution
items.abstract: Understanding and operating with scientific charts is a standard approach in data analysis, and while humans are good at interpreting such charts, open vision-language models (VLMs) are known to perform poorly when it comes to question answering based on such data types. Motivated by an initial observation that many of their errors are due to inexact answering, we raise the following natural question: how much accuracy can we recover without changing the model at all? In this paper, we study this question by searching over inference programs and the code around a "frozen" version of the model. Using ideas from autonomous evolution (famously used in AlphaEvolve), we first start from a baseline inference program, and in each round we show an LLM judge the code together with a few failures on training questions, and ask for an improving evolutionary move. As usual in autonomous evolution approaches, the candidate programs are kept in a small pool ranked by training accuracy, and the next edit is performed on top-scorers from this pool. We run this approach on three VLMs and four popular benchmarks on scientific charts, and we measure the fraction of descriptive questions whose answer exactly matches the ground truth. The accuracy improves in all experimental settings. On average, it rises from 16.6% with the starting program to 41.3% with the evolved one, and the largest single increase is 55.2 percentage points. As a side benefit, our evolved program is 3.8x faster than the starting program, because short answers are easier to grade and faster to generate. Our results demonstrate that a large part of the observed errors arise due to the inference pipeline, and that optimizing it can improve the "frozen" VLM without the need to retrain it.

items.title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
items.abstract: We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent that we use for research on problems whose answers aprogram or data can check. Each candidate solution is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox; proposers see only a public score, and a private split decides what counts. The harness itself(prompts, tools, skills, playbook, meta agent) is an editable genome, changed only through a kernel-enforced gate with held-out and cost checks. An autonomous mode goes from a plain-text goal to a verified report with no human step: an agent picks an open problem and writes its verifier, the kernel calibrates it, an adversarial agent audits it, and an agent that never sees the verifier re-checks the result. Across fourteen problems in six days, for about $180 of model usage, the system produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information: a certified depolarizing-channel threshold point p = 0.064966, a qutrit positivity frontier of 0.2910672, a 44-gate depth-6 Golay state preparation, and a stabilizer-rank bound chi(T^7) <= 10. It also cut SABRE qubit-routing overhead from 68,559 to 12,087 added gates. In hardware, it cut the energy per MAC of an open 8x8 INT8 systolic tile by 77.7% through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow, bit-exact. Three fully autonomous runs ended in honestties with public records; one audit caught a stale record, and one agent-written score pointing the wrong way went unnoticed. We report the failures as carefully: the one self-derived harness generation was rejected on cost, proposers gamed lenient scorers four times, and operator changes were decisive for several results.

items.title: Insomnia severity and multidimensional psychological well-being in Chilean correctional personnel: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Introduction Prison officers in Chile work under highly stressful and dangerous conditions characterized by prison overcrowding, violence, long shifts, and chronic exposure to stress. Shift work and irregular schedules negatively affect sleep quality and contribute to insomnia, which in turn may impair psychological well-being. Despite growing evidence on occupational stress in correctional staff, limited research has examined the relationship between sleep quality, insomnia, and psychological well-being in prison guards. Therefore, this study aimed to assess working conditions, subjective sleep quality, insomnia severity, and psychological well-being among Chilean prison officers. Methods A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted with 43 prison guards from five prisons in the Valparaíso Region, Chile. Instruments included the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), self-ratings of subjective sleep quality and the Ryff Psychological Wellbeing Scale (PWB). Sociodemographic and work-related variables were also analyzed, including sick leave, exposure to violence at work, need for mental health care, perceived organizational support, and energy drink consumption. Results Participants reported low institutional support (60.5%) and frequent sick leave (68.4%). Over one-third considered seeking psychological care (37.2%), and 53.5% reported daily energy drink consumption. Insomnia levels were moderate and clinically relevant (M = 17.87, SD = 0.91), with high dissatisfaction and functional impairment. Psychological well-being was moderate overall (M = 54.84, SD = 16.52), with higher scores in positive relationships and lower scores in environmental mastery and personal growth. No significant association was found between ISI scores and overall or subscale psychological well-being. However, insomnia was positively associated with years at the institution ( p = 0.023, r = 0.349), indicating that longer tenure relates to higher subjective insomnia severity scores. Conclusions Chilean prison officers exhibited clinically significant insomnia, moderate psychological well-being, and low perceived institutional support. Although no significant association was found between insomnia and psychological well-being, insomnia severity increased with years of service. These findings underscore the need to improve working conditions and implement policies that promote occupational health in Chilean prisons. Incorporating a gender perspective in this highly masculinized context is also recommended, as well as further research to enhance psychological well-being.

items.title: Integrating ISO 45001 and ISO 14001 Management Systems with Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction in Niger Delta Oil Operations
items.abstract: Oil operations in the Niger Delta sit inside the same floodplains, creeks and villages that host millions of residents. Hazards such as spills, fires, floods and pipeline failures rarely stop at the fence line, yet the management systems that govern them usually do. This paper argues that ISO 45001 (occupational health and safety) and ISO 14001 (environment), both built on the same high-level structure, can be deliberately extended to include community-based disaster risk reduction (CBDRR). Using a structured document-based synthesis of international standards, the UNEP Ogoniland assessment, Sendai Framework guidance and CBDRR scholarship, we develop a five-component integration framework, map it to clauses of both standards, propose indicators, and outline a three-phase implementation roadmap for operators. The paper is conceptual: it presents no new field data, though it specifies a Delphi and household-survey design for validation, and its figures are explicitly labelled as either sourced or illustrative. We conclude that clauses on context, interested parties, worker participation, emergency preparedness and improvement already provide the entry points; what is missing is a community seat at the table.

items.title: Intelligent workspaces: how AI tools are changing service models and workforce skills in academic libraries
items.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming service models, workflows, and workforce roles in academic libraries in Saudi Arabia. It examines the extent to which AI adoption influences service delivery, professional responsibilities, staff competencies, organizational readiness, and the development of intelligent library workspaces. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative descriptive design based on twenty semi-structured interviews with librarians, information technology staff, and administrative personnel working in academic libraries in Saudi Arabia. Participants were purposively selected based on their direct experience with AI-supported tools and technology-enabled library services. The interview data were analyzed thematically following Braun and Clarke's framework to identify patterns relating to AI-tool adoption, service transformation, workforce competencies, staff readiness, and implementation challenges. Findings The findings reveal four interrelated dimensions of AI-driven transformation in academic libraries. First, AI tools such as chatbots, intelligent discovery systems, automated search applications, and plagiarism-detection tools are increasingly embedded in routine library operations. Second, AI is contributing to more automated, personalized, responsive, and digitally mediated service models. Third, workforce roles are shifting toward supervisory, analytical, instructional, and technology-mediated responsibilities, increasing the need for competencies in AI literacy, digital skills, data management, system oversight, and evaluation of AI-generated outputs. Fourth, successful implementation is constrained by training gaps, uneven staff readiness, infrastructural and system-integration limitations, concerns about AI reliability, and ethical issues involving privacy, bias, misinformation, and data governance. The findings emphasize the importance of continuous professional development, reliable technological infrastructure, human oversight, and clear institutional governance mechanisms. Originality/value This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on the simultaneous transformation of library services, workflows, workforce competencies, and organizational readiness associated with AI adoption in Saudi Arabian academic libraries. By integrating the perspectives of librarians, IT personnel, and administrative staff, it extends existing research beyond individual AI applications and conceptualizes AI adoption as a broader socio-technical and workforce transformation. The study also offers practical guidance for library managers on AI competency development, responsible human–AI collaboration, organizational readiness, and ethical governance.

items.title: Intent-Preserving Adversarial User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agent Evaluation
items.abstract: Multi-turn agents are commonly evaluated with LLM-based simulated users, which can be overly cooperative and can therefore overestimate an agent's performance. We here introduce StressSim, an intent-preserving adversarial user simulator framework for stress-testing agents with challenging yet valid user interactions. StressSim optimises the simulator's high-level adversarial plan for each task instance. Candidate planner prompts are evolved with a genetic prompt-optimisation loop that uses rollout traces, granular task-completion signals, and validity feedback to favour conversations that reduce task success without changing the user's underlying goal. We evaluate the approach on the MultiWOZ dataset and the retail and airline domains from tau-bench with three target LLM agents, comparing against standard simulators and hand-designed non-collaborative user behaviours. We demonstrate the effectiveness of StressSim in exposing robustness gaps across frontier LLMs, with tau-bench pass^4 scores decreasing by up to 69% on gemini-3.8-flash and 62% on gpt-5.6-sol. StressSim maintains goal preservation performance (which decreases by at most 10%), using an optimisation budget of 20 rollouts per task. Sensitivity analysis suggests that increasing the budget further decreases task success. Overall our results demonstrate that StressSim exposes robustness gaps missed by standard and hand-designed user simulators while maintaining conversation realism. This is achieved through lightweight prompt optimisation alone, without model fine-tuning.

items.title: Interpreting LLM Scores in Peer Review: Alignment and Divergence Across Prompts, Domains, and Manuscript Features
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) scores are being studied as information for scholarly evaluation. Interpreting these scores requires evidence about agreement with human judgments and its variation across evaluation conditions. Guided by an argument-based approach to validation, we compare four LLMs on 7,083 public ICLR 2024 submissions under a standard review condition and examine ten prompt conditions using DeepSeek-V3.2. We distinguish average score divergence, paper-level absolute error, and rank correlation, then examine domain differences and adjusted manuscript-feature associations. For DeepSeek-V3.2, Area Chair guidance reduces mean rating divergence from 1.460 to 0.199 points and mean absolute error from 1.577 to 0.942, while rank correlation changes from 0.377 to 0.387. Historical references combined with downward scoring instructions yield mean divergence of 0.052 and rank correlation of 0.321. Domain differences remain after global calibration. Longer titles have positive adjusted associations with rating divergence, and formula density has negative associations across all four configurations. These findings connect score interpretation to the scoring procedure, evaluation context, and manuscript information represented in the comparison. They show why aggregate alignment, manuscript ordering, and correspondence within manuscript groups require distinct evidence when evaluating LLM-generated scholarly assessment information.

items.title: Interrogation of Retrieval Augmented Generation-Based Intelligent System for Personalized Medication Identification, Safety Assessment, and Patient Advisory
items.abstract: Wrong prescriptions are among the most common causes of patient harm that could have been avoided with medication AI assisting the interpretation of possible ambiguous drug names, dosages, frequencies, routes of administration etc. Unclear handwritten prescriptions represent a significant portion of the cases. Standard OCR can digitize prescription images, but cannot verify medication nor return clinically safe interpretations by itself. We introduce MedGuard AI, an RAG-powered AI system to personalize drug identification and patient safety alerts/notifications. The system transforms prescription text to normalized medication identities which are mapped to structured clinical data to power a patient safety use case. An entity extraction model fine-tuned on token classification tasks locates medication mentions. Dictionary-based normalization and fuzzy matching of known brand, generic, and canonical names follow. This process outputs medication candidates that the user must confirm before safety calculations can begin. Allergy, drug-drug interaction, contraindication and other medication checks are processed by deterministic rule-based engines using structured drug knowledge references. A TF-IDF based retriever operating locally augments generated explanations with extracted supporting evidence, limiting hallucinations and improving traceback. The extraction pipeline model was fine-tuned on 1,500 labeled prescriptions, resulting in an F1-score of 0.86 (macro), 0.97(weighted) and 0.98(micro) with a token accuracy of 0.98. The prototype is made of a FastAPI server, ReactJS 19 web frontend, the local retrieval database, constrained LLM deployed for explanation generation with deterministic offline fallback, PDF rendering for export of results, and 17-unit test cases. Separating deterministic parts from generative parts allows higher trust and clinical defensibility.

items.title: Intervene, Calibrate, Discover: Learning Causal Structure from Pixels
items.abstract: Learning high-level causal variables from low-level observations is a central problem for artificial intelligence. With known node semantics but an unknown graph, visual readout errors can misalign model settings with environment intervention values. We address this mismatch by pairing image readouts with verified values attained through fixed round-robin interventions. With encoder and decoder frozen, a dimension-wise invertible calibration map puts visual responses and target settings in shared numerical units. After freezing this map, the agent selects interventions to resolve graph directions and fits local mechanisms to predict consequences; inverse calibration returns counterfactual states to the decoder's original coordinates. Across Domino, Pick-and-Place, Balance, Gears, CAUSAL3D, and CausalWorld, we evaluate graph discovery, intervention consequences, and counterfactual images. Controlled domino experiments show that interventions resolve orientation ambiguity left by equal additional observations. In a matched-data domino control, calibration reduces the mean error of predicted changes in other variables within the same factual context, relative to an uncalibrated model.

items.abstract: Over the past several years, digital intraoral scanning has moved from a promising innovation to a routine part of clinical practice. This review summarizes current evidence on the accuracy of contemporary intraoral scanners, examines the technical, clinical and operator-related factors that determine the quality of a digital impression, and outlines the remaining limitations of the method. Particular attention is paid to devices released in 2024–2026 and to embedded artificial intelligence algorithms used both to improve scan quality and to support diagnosis. The analysis is based on recent systematic reviews, meta-analyses and clinical studies.

items.title: INVAR-Agri: Detecting Discrepancies in Multilingual Operator Manuals of Agricultural Implements with a Fine-Tuned LLM
items.abstract: Operator manuals of agricultural implements are delivered in many languages, and the standards require that competent persons review every translation, which makes this review the bottleneck. This paper presents a proof of concept that compares two training workflows on the same LLM, EuroLLM-1.7B-Instruct, trained on operator manuals of one manufacturer. In approach A, a back-translator translates each language version back into English, and an English reader compares it with the English version. In approach B, a checker reads the English version and the translation together, where the checker reports differences. The test sets contain errors planted in numbers, units, opposite words, obligations, negations, and conditions in 24 languages, and they include unmodified text and meaning-preserving edits for alerts and false alarms. The trained back-translator concealed many planted errors, most of all weakened obligations, while translation-quality scores rose. In contrast, the separately trained checker detected most planted errors, although it was weak for units and for number changes unlike those in training. A check by the author confirmed the concealment. In addition, a simple rule check caught the number and unit changes, but it alerted on harmless rewrites. A check of alerts on real Finnish translations showed that most alerts were false, caused by language-specific wording, so the precision on real text remains a limitation. Within this setting, a trained checker might support, not replace, the review by competent persons, and firmer conclusions need more data.

items.title: INVISIBLE EYES: PLAUSIBLE PATHWAYS FOR AI-ENABLED SURVEILLANCE IN NORTH KOREA – A SCENARIO ANALYSIS
items.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence could reshape surveillance and social control in North Korea, focusing on Pyongyang. Rather than viewing AI surveillance as a sudden rupture, it conceptualises it as a possible intensification of North Korea’s existing human-centred system, one that already includes household monitoring, workplace surveillance, mobility control, and ideological discipline. Drawing on studies of surveillance and algorithmic governance, and using the city of Urumqi in Xinjiang as an empirical reference architecture, the paper distinguishes three functions of AI-enabled surveillance: tracking, profiling, and pre-emptive policing. Using scenario analysis, the study identifies two critical uncertainties for the North Korean authorities: the level of domestic technological capacity and access to surveillance-relevant hardware, software, and expertise. It then constructs four potential scenarios for Pyongyang by 2035: the deployment of ‘symbolic’ AI, a constrained deployment of domestic AI, an import-dependent uptake, and a full AI panopticon. The paper argues that the most plausible near-term trajectory is a fragmented, import-dependent expansion of tracking and selective profiling rather than fully integrated predictive control. Despite their fragmentary nature, such systems could increase the costs for North Korean citizens engaging in unauthorised mobility, foreign media circulation, informal economic activity, and local non-compliance, while remaining constrained by energy shortages, fragmented data, bureaucratic silos, and everyday strategies of circumvention.

items.title: IoT-enabled multimodal large language model-based framework for compositional food recognition, nutrient profiling, NOVA classification, and cancer risk mitigation
items.abstract: Background Automated dietary assessment increasingly struggles to evaluate industrial food processing levels, revealing a systemic gap between the visual presentation of meals and their underlying ultra-processed food composition. Although existing dietary monitoring tools can effectively track caloric and macronutrient intake, they lack the qualitative processing assessments required to identify hidden additives and map dietary risk triage quadrants. Methods This study introduces a modular, IoT-enabled multimodal dietary decision-support framework that decouples visual food recognition, standardized database retrieval, and qualitative language reasoning for automated NOVA processing classification and 2D decision matrix mapping. Operating on isolated single-dish meal instances, the system employs a four-phase cascaded pipeline that integrates vision-language models, database retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with strict JSON schema enforcement. The platform was evaluated using the Nutrition-NOVA validation benchmark, a harmonized multimodal dataset constructed through dense vector-space semantic linkage between quantitative profiles from the Center for Food Safety database and qualitative NOVA tiers from Open Food Facts. This benchmark addresses a 75.0% metadata sparsity deficit identified in legacy repositories. Results In experimental evaluations on the Nutrition-NOVA benchmark, the baseline Qwen-VL-Max architecture achieved an adjacent accuracy of 77.7%. Furthermore, enforcing schema modularity enabled complete plug-and-play backend replaceability between commercial cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) and private, on-premises open-weight models without requiring architectural retraining. Discussion The proposed framework establishes an efficient, safety-first screening tool for digital healthcare decision support. By isolating qualitative LLM reasoning from visual perceptual noise and database metadata sparsity, the system successfully bridges the gap between intuitive meal perception and point-of-care dietary risk triage, offering a non-invasive and scalable solution for automated dietary auditing and longitudinal population health monitoring.

items.title: Keabsahan Perjanjian Melibatkan Kecerdasan Buatan (AI) Sebagai Sarana Bantu Dalam Perspektif Hukum Perikatan
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has made legal practice easier, especially when it comes to drafting agreements. AI can be used to identify hazards, generate terms, examine contracts, and offer suggestions about the content of contracts. But using AI also brings up legal questions about the legality of contracts, the legal standing of AI, and the parties' liabilities. In accordance with Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code, this study will examine the legality of contracts that incorporate AI. It will also examine the current state of AI and the effects of its application on the parties' rights, responsibilities, and liabilities under Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code. Legal materials are evaluated using a descriptive-qualitative method, and the study uses a normative-juridical approach that makes use of statutory and conceptual approaches. The results show that, as long as the four conditions for a legal agreement are satisfied, the employment of AI does not automatically make an agreement void. While humans or legal entities acting as legal subjects retain power, binding force, and legal culpability, AI is better viewed as an assisting tool. Therefore, in order to guaranty legal certainty and the protection of the parties involved, the deployment of AI necessitates human evaluation and monitoring.

items.title: Khastgir Algorithm: A Digital Development Goals-Aligned Framework for Real-Time Hallucination Detection and Reporting
items.abstract: Abstract The exponential deployment of large language models (LLMs) across commercial and public sectors in 2026 and beyond has created an urgent accountability gap that traditional IP frameworks were never designed to address. When these systems generate hallucinations around resultant data in the form of fabricated citations, non-existent precedents, or fictional technical specifications, the resulting misinformation doesn't merely distort discourse but creates chaos to perform the task again from scratch. Factually incorrect output data currently pose significant risks across critical domains including healthcare, legal systems, financial services, and public policy. The hallucination crisis forces us to confront a deeper question: what does it mean to build "responsible" technology when our most advanced creations confidently lie? Through the Khastgir Algorithm's 103 sub-modules, I've always argued that responsibility isn't a compliance checkbox but a living system of interlocking accountabilities—IP rights protecting human creativity, carbon-negative operations preserving planetary boundaries, and DAO governance ensuring no single entity monopolizes truth. Hallucinations expose the moral vacuum in models trained without such frameworks. The current expanded architecture discussed in this paper therefore treats each fabricated output as a teachable moment and not merely flagged and logged, but routed through a global network of stakeholder DAOs who collectively determine the remediation protocol, transforming error correction into a democratic exercise that strengthens rather than erodes public trust in AI systems. This paper expands the foundational Khastgir Algorithm originally designed for AI-mediated intellectual property dispute resolution and time is apt to incorporate Digital Development Goals (DDGs) as one of the governing frameworks for identifying and reporting hallucinated data in real-time. The enhanced comprehensive architecture framework integrates token-level hallucination probes, blockchain-anchored verification mechanisms, and automated reporting pipelines aligned with UNDP's Digital Strategy 2022-2025 objectives and United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The proposed framework leverages advanced machine learning techniques including attention mechanism analysis, semantic consistency validation, and cross-reference verification, combined with a permissioned blockchain architecture running on the Impula Network. items.title: Knowing When to Escalate: Disagreement Patterns for Uncertainty-Aware Content Moderation
items.abstract: Agentic content-moderation systems increasingly rely on collective judgments from LLM agents, while aggregation methods commonly treat inter-agent disagreement as a reliability problem to be removed through consensus or voting. This framing is inappropriate for value-laden tasks, where disagreement may reflect irreducible value pluralism - a distinction standard uncertainty decompositions cannot recover, since they operate on output distributions and discard the reasoning behind each judgment. We propose Reasoning Trace Divergence Analysis (RTDA), which embeds model-generated justifications from perspective-differentiated agents and classifies each case by justification similarity and conclusion agreement. The resulting four-state taxonomy isolates convergent disagreement, where agents reasoning similarly but concluding differently, as a candidate signature of value-laden conflict. On 1,000 items from the Measuring Hate Speech corpus, this structural signal predicts human annotator disagreement better than magnitude-only and output-only baselines. We contribute a design principle: condition human escalation on the structure of disagreement, not its magnitude alone, with RTDA serving as a post-processing layer for systems that already generate reasoning traces.

items.title: Knowledge flows and service encounters in digital retail: a bibliometric mapping of cross-buying and customer relationship expansion research (2000–2026)
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to map the intellectual structure, knowledge flows and thematic evolution of cross-buying and customer relationship expansion research in digital retail and service encounter contexts from 2000 to 2026. Design/methodology/approach A bibliometric science-mapping design guided by the SPAR-4-SLR protocol was adopted. Data were retrieved from Scopus using a TITLE-ABS-KEY search. After applying year, subject area, document type, language and source type filters and removing one duplicate DOI record, the final data set comprised 567 Scopus-indexed journal documents. “Bibliometrix” and “VOSviewer” were used for performance analysis, co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, keyword co-occurrence, temporal overlay, thematic mapping and thematic evolution. Findings The field is rooted in customer lifetime value, customer equity, CRM, service quality, satisfaction, loyalty and relationship marketing. Recent research fronts increasingly emphasise digital service quality, customer engagement, e-commerce, omnichannel service encounters, artificial intelligence, machine learning and predictive analytics. Thematic evolution shows a shift from firm-centric customer valuation and retention models toward digitally mediated, experience-driven and analytics-enabled relationship expansion. Practical implications Managers should treat cross-buying as a relationship-expansion outcome shaped by service quality, trust, customer experience, engagement and responsible data use, rather than only as a sales or targeting objective. Originality/value This study positions cross-buying within customer relationship expansion and provides an integrated bibliometric synthesis of its intellectual foundations, research fronts, conceptual themes and future research agenda.

items.title: La agencia de marketing aumentada por agentes: comoditización por capas, divergencia entre holdings y la brecha de atribución (2024–2026) / The agent-augmented marketing agency: layered commoditization, divergence among holding companies and the attribution gap (2024–2026)
items.abstract: El discurso dominante sobre la inteligencia artificial en el sector publicitario presenta una disyuntiva simple: las agencias que adopten IA crecerán y las que no, desaparecerán. La evidencia pública de 2024–2026 —comunicaciones de resultados, documentos de registro corporativos, planes y objetivos anunciados, documentación de las plataformas y prensa especializada— no sostiene esa lectura. Este working paper descompone la cadena de valor de la agencia en seis capas —investigación, estrategia, producción creativa, compra de medios, medición y gobernanza— y sostiene que la comoditización avanza capa a capa según tres atributos de cada tarea: si el entregable es especificable, si existe un oráculo de aceptación barato y si la acción es reversible. Definimos operativamente la comoditización como la sustitución de horas facturables por un coste marginal cercano a cero, y mostramos que la parte de la cadena que cumple los tres atributos —variantes creativas, informes, operación de pujas— no la está absorbiendo primero el agente de la agencia, sino la propia plataforma publicitaria, con productos anteriores a la ola de agentes: Meta desplegó su motor de recuperación y clasificación Andromeda en diciembre de 2024, con un aumento declarado de capacidad de modelo de 10 000× y un incremento de ROAS del 22 % reportado por la propia compañía [10]; TikTok lanzó su suite automatizada Smart+ el 7 de octubre de 2024 [11]; y Google elevó en marzo de 2025 el límite de palabras clave negativas de Performance Max a 10 000 por campaña, dejando el límite de cuenta en 1 000 [12]. El hallazgo central es negativo y afecta a la narrativa del sector: la divergencia financiera entre holdings —Publicis con un margen operativo del 18,0 % y un crecimiento orgánico del 5,8 % en 2024 [2], Havas con un crecimiento orgánico del 3,1 % y un margen EBIT ajustado del 12,9 % en 2025 [8], frente a WPP con ingresos menos costes repercutidos de 10 176 millones de libras, un −5,4 % comparable y un deterioro de fondo de comercio de 641 millones [3], Dentsu con un deterioro de 86 000 millones de yenes en el primer semestre de 2025 [6] y un recorte de en torno al 8 % de su plantilla internacional (unos 3 400 empleos) [7], y Omnicom con un objetivo de sinergias elevado a 1 500 millones de dólares tras absorber IPG [5]— no permite identificar el efecto de la adopción de IA. La composición del negocio y las operaciones corporativas son factores concurrentes cuya contribución no se estima aquí. Declaramos explícitamente que con la evidencia pública disponible no es posible separar el efecto de la IA del efecto de las fusiones, los deterioros contables y la pérdida de cuentas: es la limitación más seria de este trabajo y condiciona toda lectura causal. En el lado del consumidor, dos estudios independientes apuntan en la misma dirección —menor resonancia emocional y menor disposición a interactuar cuando se revela el origen sintético [16], [17]—, sin una magnitud del efecto cotejada en esta síntesis. Proponemos una matriz de delegación por capa, una reformulación del modelo de precios acotada por la brecha de atribución (la distancia entre el resultado que la agencia puede medir de forma creíble y el resultado por el que quiere cobrar) y una traducción de la gobernanza de marca a política ejecutable dentro del harness del agente. No aportamos experimento propio ni datos de adopción: el corpus utilizado no contiene telemetría comparable que permita identificar ese tratamiento. Palabras clave: comoditización por capas, cadena de valor de la agencia, agentes LLM en operaciones, Performance Max, Advantage+, modelización de mezcla de marketing, medición incremental, brecha de atribución, gobernanza de marca ejecutable, régimen post-cookie. English abstract: The dominant narrative about artificial intelligence in the advertising industry offers a simple dichotomy: agencies that adopt AI will grow, and those that do not will disappear. Public 2024–2026 evidence —results communications, corporate registration documents, announced plans and targets, platform documentation and trade press— does not support that reading. This working paper decomposes the agency value chain into six layers — research, strategy, creative production, media buying, measurement and governance — and argues that commoditization advances layer by layer according to three task attributes: whether the deliverable is specifiable, whether a cheap acceptance oracle exists, and whether the action is reversible. We define commoditization operationally as the substitution of billable hours by a near-zero marginal cost, and show that the portion of the chain satisfying all three attributes — creative variants, reporting, bid operation — is being absorbed first not by the agency's agent but by the advertising platform itself, through products that predate the agentic wave: Meta deployed its Andromeda retrieval and ranking engine in December 2024, with a declared 10,000× model-capacity increase and a self-reported 22% ROAS lift [10]; TikTok launched its automated Smart+ suite on 7 October 2024 [11]; and Google raised the Performance Max negative-keyword limit to 10,000 per campaign in March 2025, leaving the account-level limit at 1,000 [12]. The central finding is negative and cuts against the industry narrative: financial divergence among holding companies — Publicis at an 18.0% operating margin and 5.8% organic growth in 2024 [2], Havas at 3.1% organic growth and a 12.9% adjusted EBIT margin in 2025 [8], versus WPP with revenue less pass-through costs of £10,176m, −5.4% like-for-like and a £641m goodwill impairment [3], Dentsu with an ¥86bn impairment in the first half of 2025 [6] and a reduction of about 8% of its international workforce (some 3,400 roles) [7], and Omnicom with a synergy target raised to USD 1.5bn after absorbing IPG [5] — does not identify the effect of AI adoption. Business composition and corporate operations are concurrent factors whose contributions are not estimated here. We state explicitly that available public evidence cannot separate the effect of AI from the effects of mergers, accounting impairments and account losses: this is the paper's most serious limitation and it constrains every causal reading. On the consumer side, two independent studies point the same way — lower emotional resonance and lower willingness to engage when synthetic origin is disclosed [16], [17] — without an effect-size estimate verified in this synthesis. We propose a per-layer delegation matrix, a pricing model bounded by the attribution gap (the distance between the outcome an agency can credibly measure and the outcome it wishes to be paid for), and a translation of brand governance into executable policy inside the agent harness. We contribute no original experiment and no adoption data: the corpus used contains no comparable telemetry that identifies that treatment. Keywords: layered commoditization, agency value chain, LLM agents in operations, Performance Max, Advantage+, marketing mix modeling, incrementality measurement, attribution gap, executable brand governance, post-cookie regime. items.title: La gestion intégrée des risques de l'intelligence artificielle : enjeux techniques, réglementaires et sociotechniques pour la gouvernance des systèmes d'information
items.abstract: Résumé L’intégration croissante de l’intelligence artificielle dans les systèmes d’information transforme le traitement et l’exploitation des données, tout en exposant les organisations à de nouveaux risques techniques, réglementaires et sociotechniques. La gestion de ces risques constitue ainsi un enjeu important pour une utilisation sûre et responsable de ces technologies. Cette étude vise à examiner comment les organisations peuvent identifier, évaluer et maîtriser les risques liés à l’intelligence artificielle en articulant les dimensions techniques, réglementaires et sociotechniques, souvent abordées séparément. L’étude repose sur une synthèse narrative de la littérature récente. L’analyse est organisée autour de trois ensembles de travaux portant sur les vulnérabilités techniques et les mécanismes de défense, la gouvernance de l’intelligence artificielle et la conformité réglementaire, ainsi que les risques sociotechniques et éthiques. Les résultats montrent que les réponses techniques réduisent certaines vulnérabilités sans garantir une protection durable face à l’évolution des menaces et peuvent entraîner des arbitrages, notamment en matière de confidentialité. Les cadres de gouvernance offrent des repères importants, mais leur mise en œuvre organisationnelle demeure complexe. Les risques sociotechniques restent, quant à eux, insuffisamment intégrés aux processus d’évaluation et de décision. L’étude met en évidence une fragmentation persistante entre ces différentes approches. Elle souligne l’intérêt d’une approche intégrée de la gestion des risques, associant l’évaluation continue des vulnérabilités, une gouvernance adaptée au niveau de risque, la conformité réglementaire et la prise en compte des conséquences sociotechniques dans les systèmes d’information. Mots clés : intelligence artificielle ; gestion des risques ; gouvernance de l’IA ; systèmes d’information ; conformité réglementaire ; risques sociotechniques. Abstract The growing integration of artificial intelligence into information systems is transforming the processing and use of data while exposing organizations to new technical, regulatory, and sociotechnical risks. Managing these risks has therefore become an important challenge for the safe and responsible use of these technologies. This study examines how organizations can identify, assess, and manage the risks associated with artificial intelligence by bringing together technical, regulatory, and sociotechnical dimensions that are often addressed separately. The study is based on a narrative review of recent literature. The analysis is structured around three main areas: technical vulnerabilities and defense mechanisms, artificial intelligence governance and regulatory compliance, and sociotechnical and ethical risks. The findings show that technical responses can reduce certain vulnerabilities without ensuring lasting protection against evolving threats and may involve trade-offs, particularly regarding privacy. Governance frameworks provide important guidance, but their implementation within organizations remains challenging. Meanwhile, sociotechnical risks are still insufficiently integrated into risk assessment and decision-making processes. The study highlights persistent fragmentation among these approaches. It underlines the value of an integrated risk management approach combining continuous vulnerability assessment, risk-proportionate governance, regulatory compliance, and consideration of sociotechnical consequences within information systems. Keywords : artificial intelligence; risk management; artificial intelligence governance; information systems; regulatory compliance; sociotechnical risks.

items.title: LA INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL EN LA INNOVACIÓN EMPRESARIAL: APLICACIÓN DE LA GAMIFICACIÓN EN LA FORMACIÓN CORPORATIVA, ESTUDIO DE CASO
items.abstract: La transformación digital plantea nuevas exigencias para la formación del capital humano corporativo y evidencia limitaciones en las estrategias tradicionales de capacitación frente a las necesidades de aprendizaje ágil, colaborativo y personalizado del entorno empresarial contemporáneo. En este contexto, la convergencia entre inteligencia artificial (IA) y gamificación constituye una alternativa innovadora para fortalecer los procesos de formación. El presente estudio analiza el impacto de la IA en la innovación de procesos, con énfasis en la aplicación de la gamificación y las experiencias inmersivas como estrategias para la capacitación y la optimización del aprendizaje. Se presenta un estudio de caso aplicado a una entidad financiera de Quito, Ecuador, mediante un serious game orientado al fortalecimiento de la cultura organizacional a través de dinámicas colaborativas. Se empleó un enfoque metodológico mixto, basado en entrevistas semiestructuradas, análisis documental, observación de entornos y pruebas de aplicabilidad. Los resultados evidencian un alto nivel de acceso técnico y usabilidad inicial, dado que la mayoría de los participantes logró acceder, instalar e interactuar con la aplicación sin inconvenientes significativos. No obstante, se identificó una brecha entre la autopercepción de los participantes y su desempeño real durante la dinámica del juego. Se concluye que, aunque la gamificación apoyada por IA presenta viabilidad técnica, requiere mejoras en el diseño comunicacional y pedagógico para favorecer la comprensión de los roles y la colaboración efectiva. El estudio aporta evidencia sobre esta brecha y orientaciones para el diseño de serious games aplicados a la formación corporativa. Para explicar la brecha identificada, se proponen tres métricas exploratorias: Perception–Performance Gap (PPG), Behavioral Calibration Ratio (BCR) y Technical–Pedagogical Drop (TPD). Palabra clave: gamificación, innovación tecnológica, inteligencia artificial, negocios Abstract Digital transformation poses new demands on corporate human capital development and highlights limitations in traditional training strategies in addressing the need for agile, collaborative, and personalized learning in the contemporary business environment. In this context, the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and gamification represents an innovative alternative for strengthening training processes. This study analyzes the impact of AI on process innovation, with an emphasis on the application of gamification and immersive experiences as strategies for training and learning optimization. A case study was conducted in a financial institution in Quito, Ecuador, using a serious game aimed at strengthening organizational culture through collaborative dynamics. A mixed-methods approach was employed, based on semi-structured interviews, document analysis, environmental observation, and applicability testing. The results indicate a high level of initial technical access and usability, as most participants were able to access, install, and interact with the application without significant difficulties. However, a gap was identified between participants’ self-perception and their actual performance during the game dynamics. The study concludes that, although AI-supported gamification demonstrates technical feasibility, improvements in communicational and pedagogical design are required to promote role comprehension and effective collaboration. The study provides evidence of this gap and offers guidelines for the design of serious games applied to corporate training. To explain the identified gap, three exploratory metrics are proposed: Perception–Performance Gap (PPG), Behavioral Calibration Ratio (BCR), and Technical–Pedagogical Drop (TPD). items.title: LADDER: Diagnosing Domain-Level Self-Assessment Under Noisy Feedback
items.abstract: Knowing when they are reliable is essential for language models to support human-AI collaboration. Yet interaction feedback is not always complete or correct, and may mislead models' understanding of their own capabilities. We introduce LADDER to study how language models assess themselves under unreliable feedback. Our findings show that models can accurately report supplied performance information while still struggling to form trustworthy self-assessments from interaction experience. Apparently accurate assessments can obscure capability differences and do not necessarily predict future task performance. These findings suggest that trustworthy self-assessment should be evaluated against observed task performance and its predictive value. Our study provides empirical evidence of the limits of model self-knowledge and a basis for evaluating capability awareness in reliable human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Language-based assessments for experienced well-being: accuracy and external validity across behaviors, traits, and states
items.abstract: Abstract While language is central to human communication, psychological science has relied on self-reported rating scales for decades because it was difficult to quantify language effectively. Large language models (LLMs) have changed that in recent years. Here, we used LLMs with machine learning to compare traditional ratings against language-based responses (short essays and descriptive words) of experienced well-being over 12 weeks from 764 individuals from an overburdened population highly exposed to emotional experience, U.S. hospitality workers. While accuracies were comparable by internal criterion (across 9 affective traits; words r = .53 vs. .51 for ratings), both language formats doubled the ratings’ accuracy (up to r = .18 and .24 for words and essays, respectively) across 24 external criteria: traits, demographics, and behavior. Beyond improved accuracy, language responses offered psychological insights: words provided concise emotional nuances, whereas essays encompassed broad life contexts. Though each language-based format differed in strengths and weaknesses, both demonstrated greater information-richness than traditional rating scales.

items.title: Large Language Model-Based Sentiment Analysis for Public Transit Satisfaction Using Trip Chain Data
items.abstract: This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing public transit user satisfaction by processing unstructured, voice-derived trip chain data. Traditional survey methods often do not capture the contextual and real time aspects of user experience. To address this limitation, this study employs large language models and natural language processing techniques to analyze trip-related feedback collected from 5,000 public transit users. Sentiment scores were extracted from a station-labeled subset of the data set and applied to a broader corpus to assess satisfaction levels across subway stations in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Using a combination of sentiment analysis and K-means clustering, this study categorized 102 subway stations into three groups: (1) High Satisfaction Station Group; (2) Low Satisfaction Station Group; and (3) Moderate Satisfaction Station Group. These clusters were the basis for grouping stations, and user feedback on transit experiences was summarized for each station within its respective cluster. This approach enables the identification of low-satisfaction transit stations requiring immediate attention, as well as moderate-satisfaction transit stations where service equity must be addressed. The proposed methodology offers a practical alternative to traditional survey-based assessments by leveraging unstructured public transit users’ data. With further refinement and institutional support, this approach can enhance data-driven, user-centered transit planning and contribute to broader improvements in urban mobility.

items.title: Large Language Models and Applied Surgical Anatomy: Evaluation of Anatomical Reasoning in Expert‐Derived Plastic Surgery Scenarios
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into medical education, research, and clinical decision‐support applications; however, their ability to apply anatomical knowledge in clinically relevant surgical scenarios remains insufficiently studied. This study evaluated and compared the performance of six contemporary LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, and Manus) using 25 expert‐derived applied surgical anatomy scenarios relevant to plastic surgery. Scenarios were developed by an expert panel consisting of one associate professor of anatomy and two plastic surgeons. Responses were generated using a standardized prompt and assessed with a structured scoring rubric evaluating anatomical accuracy, clinical reasoning, completeness, and safety, with a maximum score of 10 points per question. Critical errors were additionally assessed. Significant differences in overall performance were observed among models (Friedman χ 2 = 43.51, p < 0.001). ChatGPT achieved the maximum aggregate score (250/250), followed by Gemini (248/250), DeepSeek (241/250), Copilot (240/250), Claude (235/250), and Manus (219/250). Critical errors were infrequent and were confined to a reconstructive vascular physiology scenario: DeepSeek, Claude, and Manus each demonstrated one observed critical error, whereas ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot demonstrated none. Although all evaluated models demonstrated excellent performance, clinically significant anatomical misconceptions persisted despite high aggregate scores. These findings demonstrate strong performance by the tested LLMs on this specific scenario‐based benchmark, while also identifying clinically meaningful anatomical errors in a subset of responses. Future evaluations should focus not only on overall accuracy but also on clinically meaningful error patterns that may influence surgical decision‐making. Importantly, substantial ceiling effects limited discrimination among high‐performing models, and the findings should therefore be interpreted as performance on this specific benchmark rather than as evidence of a general hierarchy of anatomical reasoning capability.

items.title: Large language models in personalized oncology
items.abstract: Background . Large language models are considered a promising tool for personalized oncology; however, their role in the analysis of molecular data and treatment selection should be clearly distinguished from the functions of specialized predictive models. Objective . To systematize the potential applications of large language models in personalized oncology, primarily for the interpretation of clinical, genomic, and transcriptomic data and of predictions of tumor chemo- and radiosensitivity. Methods . We performed a narrative review of publications identified in PubMed and Google Scholar, with the search updated through July 1, 2026. Original studies and reviews on medical LLM applications, foundation models for genomic and transcriptomic data, clinical decision support, and prediction of anticancer treatment sensitivity were considered. Results . The most justified approach is to use a language model as an interface layer: a specialized machine-learning or deep-learning model calculates the prediction, while the language model generates an explanation, compares the result with clinical guidelines, and indicates limitations. The main risks include unreliable responses, insufficient reproducibility, weak external validation, and legal constraints. Conclusion . A clinically promising architecture separates computation from explanation: the language model does not prescribe treatment autonomously but links molecular data, a validated predictive model, and the physician.

items.title: Leadership as a Service? Delegating Leadership Functions to Agentic AI—Boundaries, Risks and Accountabilities
items.abstract: Leadership is increasingly delivered, in part, by software. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems now monitor team activity, coordinate work across people and tools, schedule and assign tasks, deliver feedback and performance nudges, and broker information between leaders and followers — functions that organisations once obtained only from human managers. This has prompted the suggestion that leadership itself is becoming a service: a set of functions that can be specified, subscribed to and supplied by systems rather than embodied in persons. This conceptual paper examines that suggestion critically. Drawing on functional leadership theory, the automation–augmentation paradox, and the literature on algorithmic management and trust in AI, I develop a function-by-delegability framework that classifies five leadership functions — sensing and monitoring, coordination, deciding and allocating, developing and giving feedback, and representing and meaning-making — according to how far each can responsibly be delegated to agentic systems. I argue that delegability is governed less by technical capability than by accountability: I introduce the accountability floor, the principle that functions whose delegation would break the chain of accountability may be automated in execution but never in ownership. I identify four risks of delegation — legitimacy and follower trust, bias at scale, accountability gaps, and erosion of the leadership pipeline — propose governance and design principles, and derive three propositions for empirical research.

items.title: Leading Inclusively: Universal Design Principles in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Modern organizational leaders increasingly encounter artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in their workplaces, creating both opportunities and challenges for inclusive leadership. This chapter introduces Universal Design for Learning (UDL) as a framework for navigating these technological changes while maintaining human-centered approaches to inclusion. UDL’s three core principles – multiple means of representation, engagement, and action/expression – provide leaders with practical strategies for creating flexible workplace systems that benefit all employees. When thoughtfully implemented, AI technologies can support these principles through personalized learning experiences, enhanced accessibility features, and improved communication tools. However, the chapter cautions leaders to ensure that technology is amplifying rather than replacing human judgment and cultural competence. The chapter addresses critical considerations for leaders, including the risks of algorithmic bias, the limitations of automated solutions in complex interpersonal situations, and the importance of maintaining employee agency and choice. It examines common implementation barriers – from cost concerns to misconceptions about technology as a cure-all for inclusion challenges – while demonstrating that UDL principles require minimal investment and generate significant returns. Through examination of both opportunities and pitfalls, leaders learn to distinguish between technological applications that enhance inclusion and those that may inadvertently create barriers. The chapter provides actionable guidance for implementing UDL principles in technology-enhanced environments, positioning inclusive leadership capabilities as essential competencies for organizational success regardless of technological context.

items.title: Learning to Remember: Advances in Memory Mechanisms for Large Language Models
items.abstract: Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

items.title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but often require many decoding rounds to complete a response. Efficient generation depends not only on which tokens are easy to predict, but also on how committing to them helps predict the remaining positions. A highly predictable token may provide little useful context, while revealing a less predictable token can help several other positions become predictable sooner. We propose dSpark, a new schedule distillation-based framework for learning when to commit tokens for faster diffusion language generation. To achieve this, we construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal makes other positions easier to predict, reducing uncertainty earlier in decoding. We then distill these schedules into the model to enable faster parallel sampling, with a KL-divergence regularizer to help preserve generation quality. We extensively evaluate our approach across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. On GSM8K, our method achieves remarkable 10.12$\times$ and 5.12$\times$ speedups over the various baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark.

items.title: Legal Priorities for the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Their Implementation in the Sphere of Education
items.abstract: The paper examines the conceptual foundations of the legal regulation of artificial intelligence and the possibilities of their application to the education system. The initial premise of the work is the proposition that AI has ceased to be a private technical instrument and has turned into an infrastructural technology that defines a new socio-political era and generates constitutional challenges of a systemic, synergetic and existential nature. The author identifies the key threats: the substitution of democratic institutions by algorithmic governance, technologically conditioned inequality and algorithmic discrimination, micro-manipulation of the information flow, and the concentration of power resources among the holders of algorithms. As a meta-threat, the challenge to the socio-humanistic paradigm is considered, associated with the choice between transhumanism and classical humanism. By way of discussion, eight principles of the legal regulation of AI are formulated: state strategic guidance and technological integrity; guaranteed protection of the affected person and enhanced liability; "human in the loop" in critical decisions; anthropological priority; digital equality and the prohibition of discrimination; respect for dignity and non-interference in the private sphere; managed transparency; technological neutrality and anticipatory regulation. Further, these principles are projected onto the sphere of education. The author distinguishes two modalities of the use of AI — "a simulator for the mind" and "a prosthesis for laziness" — and shows that legal regulation must establish the boundaries of the permissible application of the technology. The legal risks of algorithmic assessment are analyzed, along with the problem of the right to explanation and the protection of the student from unfounded accusations, digital inequality in access to AI tools, threats to privacy and dignity, as well as the question of the status of the educator as a condition for the humanistic development of AI. A conclusion is drawn regarding the necessity of building a system of requirements for transparency, accountability, equality of access and the preservation of human control in critical decisions.

items.title: LifeUML: A Declarative Domain-Specific Language and Mathematical Formulation for Human Mobility and Career Architecture
items.abstract: Cross-border mobility and career pivoting represent high-stakes, multi-variable optimization challenges traditionally hindered by qualitative ambiguity, subjective counseling, and disconnected legal-financial silos. In this paper, we introduce LifeUML, a formal, declarative domain-specific language (DSL) and deterministic mathematical formulation engineered to model human life trajectories, cross-border solvency runway, and global immigration feasibility. Inspired by the declarative abstraction paradigms of UML and PlantUML, LifeUML enables autonomous AI agents and individuals to compile human aspirations into structured Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) that are evaluated in-browser against empirical psychometrics (IPIP Big-Five, Holland RIASEC) and verified 2026 sovereign statutory immigration gazettes across 40 jurisdictions. We formalize four core computational metrics: (1) the Life Mobility Index (LMI), evaluating legal solvency margins, emergency cash runways, fiscal retention, and cross-cultural adaptability; (2) the AI Transformation Quotient (AX-Q), quantifying autonomous digital leverage; (3) the Dream Convergence Index (DCI), modeling high-dimensional cosine aptitude alignment against target innovation clusters; and (4) an exponential temporal willpower decay model (C(t) = C0 * exp(-lambda * t)) that enforces deterministic action-locking. We further delineate comprehensive legal and ethical safeguards: a clean-room TypeScript parser ensuring copyright independence, public-domain psychometric foundations that bypass proprietary trademark liabilities, statutory delta calculations that prevent the unauthorized practice of law (UPL), and zero-server client-side execution complying with EU AI Act (2024/1689) high-risk employment exemptions.

items.abstract: Digital literacy has become an important competence for university students writing academic papers, particularly in the final semester when they prepare articles, research proposals, or undergraduate theses. Digital literacy involves more than operating devices; it also includes searching for information, evaluating source credibility, managing references, composing texts, and using technology ethically. This article examines how digital literacy supports the academic writing skills of eighth-semester students through a literature review. A narrative literature review was conducted by examining relevant journal articles available online. Sources were selected based on topical relevance, their connection to higher education students, and the availability of bibliographic information and accessible abstracts or full texts. The review indicates that digital literacy supports writing through access to scholarly sources, information evaluation, the use of word-processing and reference-management applications, and more efficient revision. These benefits, however, require critical thinking, knowledge of academic conventions, and ethical technology use, including the use of artificial intelligence. Therefore, digital literacy development should be integrated with reading habits, writing practice, lecturer guidance, and academic integrity.

items.title: LLM Hallucination Detection via Low-rank Multilinear Decomposition
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate fluent yet factually incorrect responses, raising concerns about their reliability. Recent hallucination detectors increasingly exploit internal representations, but extracting informative signals from high-dimensional hidden states remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on selected activations or pooling-based compression, potentially overlooking discriminative information distributed across Transformer layers, feature modes, and tokens. We propose LOTUS (Low-rank Order-statistic TUcker-based Subspace learning), a multilinear low-rank decomposition framework for hallucination detection that extracts compact representations from LLM hidden states while reducing dependence on labeled data. Our approach first summarizes variable-length token representations using complementary statistical descriptors that capture peak activations, activation distributions, and cross-layer changes. We then leverage low-rank multilinear decomposition to extract compact representations that capture the underlying structure of LLM hidden states, which are subsequently used to train a lightweight hallucination classifier. Experiments across multiple LLMs and question-answering benchmarks demonstrate improved hallucination detection performance over recent state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: LLM-Based Agentic AI in Manufacturing: A Scoping Review of Applications, System Designs and Evaluation Practices
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used in manufacturing to design products, plan production, diagnose faults and operate equipment, but their designs and evaluations remain difficult to compare. We analyse 164 studies identified through Scopus, Web of Science and IEEE Xplore to examine manufacturing applications, agentic system designs and evaluation practices, and to identify where evaluation coverage falls short of the evidence that these task and design types would require. We propose taxonomies of applications, agentic designs and evaluation practices, and relate task and design characteristics to the evidence required to assess them. The findings reveal an imbalance between assessing output quality and verifying whether outputs satisfy manufacturing requirements. For planning and decision-making systems, executability and constraint compliance receive limited evaluation, while most evidence comes from offline data or simulation. Limited assessment of safety, stability across repeated runs and performance in industrial settings leaves a gap between demonstrated task performance and evidence of reliable operation under manufacturing conditions. The resulting taxonomies and evidence requirements help researchers select evaluations suited to each manufacturing use case and distinguish demonstrated task performance from evidence of reliable operation.

items.title: LLM-Enhanced Heterogeneous Graph Learning with Business Semantics for Financial Fraud Detection
items.abstract: Financial fraud detection increasingly relies on heterogeneous transaction graphs, in which entities such as cards and merchants play distinct business roles and the risk meaning of an attribute depends on the entity's role: a high transaction volume may be routine for a merchant but unusual for a card. Heterogeneous graph neural networks preserve typed entities and relations but typically treat these attributes as role-agnostic inputs and leave their business meaning implicit. Meanwhile, most existing methods integrating large language models (LLMs) with graphs focus on homogeneous graphs or heterogeneous graphs with naturally available textual attributes, leaving their use on transaction graphs with structured attributes underexplored. To address this issue, we propose SemHGT, an LLM-enhanced framework that interprets structured attributes according to entity roles and makes the business semantics explicit in three stages: (1) role-aware prompts elicit risk-related business descriptions from node attributes, and a text encoder maps them to semantic vectors that enrich node representations; (2) semantic similarity guides multi-round sampling of target-specific path instances under transaction-to-transaction schemas; (3) schema-level tokens that combine local path evidence with global neighbor summaries are processed together with the target transaction by a unified transformer. Across three benchmark datasets, SemHGT leads the evaluated baselines on most dataset--metric comparisons. Further analyses provide additional evidence for the effectiveness of SemHGT's design and clarify how its semantic modeling and evidence selection contribute to fraud detection. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SemHGT-528A/.

items.title: LongSearchEval: Evaluating Long-Horizon Web Search Capabilities of Large Language Models via a Trajectory-Aware Agent Framework with Failure-Node Localization
items.abstract: Long-horizon web search requires LLM-based agents to integrate information across web pages through extended interactions under task-specific constraints. Evaluating this capability is important not only for measuring final answer quality, but also for assessing whether an agent acquires, verifies, and uses evidence reliably over extended interactions. Existing evaluations, however, mainly rely on simulated trajectories or on post-hoc trajectories reconstructed from final answers, rather than on retained real interaction traces, which limits the fidelity of behavioral assessment and weakens support for fine-grained error localization. To address this gap, we introduce LONGSEARCHEVAL, a trajectory-aware agent evaluation framework that combines a unified agent execution protocol with source constrained outcome verification and retrospective failure-node localization. Stage 1 verifies answer groups against agent-cited webpages without human-authored gold answers; Stage 2 audits normalized rounds and links flagged failure nodes to incorrect answer groups. We evaluate 16 models from eight families on 100 tasks, yielding 1,600 retained runs and 6,545 automatically flagged failure nodes. Trajectory collection and evaluation required 1,037 and 318 hours of cumulative runtime, respectively. Human validation yields 94.50% agreement on supplied answer-group labels and 98.11% feature-correspondence precision for audited round-group links. Together, outcome scores and linked trajectory evidence support controlled model comparison and retrospective inspection of answer-related content.
